title: 1.1 Sources and conventions
text: MCF-stack collects special solutions of mean curvature flow in four categories: self-shrinkers, translators, self-expanders, and other special flows. This introduction and those four categories form the reading collection. Each example records its equation or construction, source-supported geometric properties, and a picture. Remark 1.1.1 (The source editions) . 912105D5B712 References identify the original papers or the exact supplied editions. Citations distinguish printed page numbers from PDF page numbers and retain original theorem numbers. The source inventory records file hashes and which passages have been checked; an inventoried paper has not necessarily been read. Original PDFs and extracted text are not redistributed. Construction and classification results cited from the literature retain external proofs unless a calculation is supplied here. Remark 1.1.2 (Mean curvature flow and normalization) . 4EDA6AEDEA07 For a smooth immersion $X:M^ n\times I\to \mathbb R^ N$, mean curvature flow is the geometric equation \[  (\partial _ tX)^\perp =\vec H,  \] where $\vec H$ is the trace of the second fundamental form and $\perp $ means normal projection. For hypersurfaces we use $H=\operatorname {div}_ M\nu $ and $\vec H=-H\nu $. Thus the outward normal of a round sphere has positive scalar mean curvature, and the sphere shrinks. For a smooth closed evolving submanifold, \[  \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname {Area}(M_ t)=-\int _{M_ t}|\vec H|^2\, d\mu _ t.  \] Our self-shrinkers satisfy $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$ and generate $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$. Self-expanders satisfy $\vec H=X^\perp /2$ and generate $M_ t=\sqrt t\, \Sigma $ for $t>0$. A translator satisfies $\vec H=V^\perp $ for a constant velocity $V$, with $M_ t=\Sigma +tV$. The translator pictures use upward unit speed unless stated otherwise. Dimensions, domains, scales, and time intervals are specified in each entry. Remark 1.1.3 (Scope and illustrations) . 57833B199F67 The current collection contains 52 example families: 25 shrinkers, 13 translators, 6 expanders, and 8 other special flows. The last category includes stationary solutions, ancient solutions, and other distinguished evolutions. Ancient means defined for all $t<T$ for some finite $T$; eternal means defined for all real times. Neither condition implies that the solution is a soliton. Explicit formulas are distinguished from implicit equations, ODE constructions, and asymptotic profiles. Every example has a figure. Interactive three-dimensional models allow rotation and zoom; higher-dimensional examples use projections, profiles, or schematics. Captions distinguish exact geometry, numerical ODE approximations, and schematic drawings, and identify truncated noncompact ends. These pictures do not replace the cited existence results. The collection is a growing reference, not an exhaustive classification or a formally verified library.

title: 2.1 Round shrinking spheres
text: Throughout this collection, the normalized self-shrinker equation is $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and a normalized shrinker $\Sigma $ generates $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $, $-\infty <t<0$. The standard examples appear in [ CM12 ] , pp. 757–759, and [ CatDLN2018 ] , Section 3.3, PDF p. 8. Example 2.1.1 (Round shrinking spheres) . 5D6AFC4ECF1B For an integer $n\geq 1$, an extinction time $T\in \mathbb R$, and a center $a\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$, the exact family is \[  M_ t=\{ a+\sqrt{2n(T-t)}\, \omega :\omega \in S^ n(1)\} , \qquad -\infty <t<T.  \] The centered normalized slice is $S^ n(\sqrt{2n})$ at $t=-1$. These are smooth compact embedded hypersurfaces without boundary, complete and proper, with topology $S^ n$ and full rotational symmetry. The case $n=1$ is the shrinking circle in the plane. With outward normal and $H=\operatorname {div}\nu $, all principal curvatures are $1/\sqrt{2n(T-t)}$. Thus the flow is strictly convex, $H=\sqrt{n/(2(T-t))}$ and $|A|^2=1/(2(T-t))$. It becomes extinct at $a$ in a Type I singularity at time $T$. The round sphere is entropy stable and $F$-stable, where $F$-stability allows the Gaussian center and scale to vary. These are the stability notions in [ CM12 ] , Theorems 0.12 and 0.16; stability of Gaussian area with center and scale fixed is a different question. The normalized Gaussian integral gives \[  \lambda (S^ n(\sqrt{2n})) =(4\pi )^{-n/2}(2n)^{n/2}e^{-n/2}|S^ n(1)|.  \] In particular, a two-sphere has entropy $4/e$. The three-dimensional picture is the exact surface for $n=2$; for other dimensions a round profile represents the symmetry reduction.

title: 2.4 Generalized shrinking cylinders
text: The cylinder family is recorded in [ CM12 ] , pp. 758–759. The spherical factor and the number of Euclidean directions are independent discrete parameters. Example 2.4.1 (Generalized shrinking cylinders) . D20709465D01 Let $n\geq 2$ and $1\leq k<n$. In $\mathbb R^{k+1}\times \mathbb R^{n-k}=\mathbb R^{n+1}$ the exact flow is \[  M_ t=S^ k(\sqrt{2k(-t)})\times \mathbb R^{n-k},\qquad -\infty <t<0.  \] Equivalently, $(\omega ,z)\mapsto (\sqrt{2k(-t)}\, \omega ,z)$, with $\omega \in S^ k(1)$ and $z\in \mathbb R^{n-k}$, is a normal parametrization of the flow. These are complete, proper, noncompact embedded hypersurfaces without boundary, with topology $S^ k\times \mathbb R^{n-k}$ and polynomial area growth. Their symmetries include $O(k+1)$ on the spherical factor and all Euclidean isometries in the axial factor. There are $k$ positive principal curvatures $1/\sqrt{2k(-t)}$ and $n-k$ zero principal curvatures. Hence they are mean convex and weakly convex, and $|A|^2=1/(2(-t))$. At time zero the spherical factor collapses onto the axial subspace. Topologically there are two ends if $n-k=1$, and one end if $n-k\geq 2$. Each end has exactly the displayed product geometry. They are entropy stable among the complete embedded hypersurfaces considered by [ CM12 ] , but are not $F$-stable when $1\leq k<n$; see Theorems 0.12 and 0.16. The Euclidean factor leaves entropy unchanged: $\lambda (M_{-1})=\lambda (S^ k(\sqrt{2k}))$. For the round cylinder in $\mathbb R^3$, this is $\sqrt{2\pi /e}$. For $n=2$, $k=1$, an interactive picture displays an exact finite window of the infinite cylinder. End caps are not part of the solution.

title: 2.2 Planes through the shrinker center
text: Planes are stationary solutions that also satisfy the shrinker equation; see [ CatDLN2018 ] , Sections 2.5 and 3.3, and [ CM12 ] , Theorem 0.16. Example 2.2.1 (Planes through the shrinker center) . 97FD822B6630 Let $P$ be an $n$-dimensional linear subspace of $\mathbb R^ N$, where $1\leq n<N$. Then \[  M_ t=P,\qquad -\infty <t<\infty , \qquad \vec H=0,\quad X^\perp =0.  \] Thus $P$ is both a stationary flow and a normalized self-shrinker. An affine plane is a shrinker centered at any point of that plane; it satisfies the centered equation at the origin only if it contains the origin. The inclusion is complete, proper, embedded, flat, noncompact and boundaryless, with topology $\mathbb R^ n$ and Euclidean volume growth. It has two ends for $n=1$ and one end for $n\geq 2$. The solution has no finite singular time. The identity $\sqrt{-t}\, P=P$ does not describe a geometric collapse. Its entropy is exactly one. In codimension one it is entropy stable and $F$-stable under the notions in [ CM12 ] ; no conclusion about a different constrained variation problem is intended. The picture shows a bounded patch of a plane in $\mathbb R^3$. Its boundary is a viewing boundary, not a boundary of the flow.

title: 2.3 Abresch–Langer closed shrinking curves
text: The closed planar curves are classified by [ CatAL1986 ] . The supplied sources record the curvature conservation laws in [ CatDLN2018 ] , Theorem 1, PDF pp. 5–6, and the rotation-index description in [ CatCMComplexity2020 ] , Section 6.3, supplied PDF p. 22. Example 2.3.1 (Abresch–Langer closed shrinking curves) . 55D5743A6941 Besides the round circle, there are noncircular closed immersed curves $\gamma _{m,\ell }\subset \mathbb R^2$, indexed primitively by coprime positive integers satisfying \[  \frac12<\frac m\ell <\frac1{\sqrt2}.  \] Here $m$ is the rotation index and $\ell $ is the number of periods of the curvature. Their flows are $\sqrt{-t}\, \gamma _{m,\ell }$ for $t<0$. An ODE description in the normalization of this collection is \[  \kappa _{\theta \theta }+\kappa =\frac1{2\kappa },\qquad \kappa >0,\qquad \kappa _\theta ^2+\kappa ^2-\log \kappa =E.  \] Choose the nonconstant periodic solution with curvature period $2\pi m/\ell $. With $T(\theta )=(\cos \theta ,\sin \theta )$ and $N(\theta )=(-\sin \theta ,\cos \theta )$, reconstruction gives \[  X(\theta )=2\kappa _\theta T(\theta )-2\kappa N(\theta ), \qquad \theta \in \mathbb R/(2\pi m\mathbb Z).  \] This is an ODE construction with a closing condition, not a closed elementary formula for $\kappa $. The domain is $S^1$. These are compact, complete, proper immersions with self-intersections. Their curvature is positive after orienting the curve, so they are locally strictly convex; their images do not bound convex embedded domains. The round circle is the only embedded closed shrinking curve. The noncircular curves have finite entropy strictly greater than two, as recorded in [ CatCMComplexity2020 ] , Section 6.3. The conservation law $\kappa e^{-|X|^2/4}=C>0$ relates curvature to distance from the shrinking center. Compactness makes the shrinking flow a Type I flow becoming extinct at the origin. The interactive figure starts with $(m,\ell )=(2,3)$. Enter other coprime indices in the stated range, or use the example buttons, to compute more numerical profiles. The viewer supports $m,\ell \leq 100$ and reports the numerical closing gap. This display limit is not a restriction of the classification theorem. The static drawing and printed figure show $(2,3)$. These computations illustrate the closing condition; their residuals are not certified error bounds.

title: 2.5 Angenent's shrinking torus
text: Angenent constructs an embedded rotational self-shrinker with topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$ for each $n\geq 2$ in [ CatAngenent1992 ] . We use the normalized profile equation from [ CatDLN2018 ] , Section 3.3 and equation (5.2), PDF pp. 8 and 14. Example 2.5.1 (Angenent's shrinking torus) . 10374A017921 There is a simple closed profile $s\mapsto (x(s),r(s))$ in $r>0$ whose rotation gives \[  X(s,\omega )=(x(s),r(s)\omega )\in \mathbb R\times \mathbb R^ n, \qquad \omega \in S^{n-1}(1).  \] For Euclidean arclength $s$ and tangent angle $\alpha $, the profile solves \[  x'=\cos \alpha ,\qquad r'=\sin \alpha ,\qquad \alpha '=\left(\frac{n-1}{r}-\frac r2\right)\cos \alpha +\frac x2\sin \alpha .  \] Equivalently, it is a closed geodesic of $r^{2(n-1)}e^{-(x^2+r^2)/2}(dx^2+dr^2)$ on $r>0$. The theorem selects a closed orbit by shooting; the profile is not given by a closed formula. Its flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $, $t<0$. The hypersurface is compact, embedded, complete and proper, with topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$, rotational $O(n)$ symmetry and reflection symmetry across $x=0$. When $n=2$ it is a torus in $\mathbb R^3$. It is not mean convex. Indeed, the compact embedded mean-convex classification in [ CM12 ] , Theorem 0.17, would force a sphere. It shrinks to the origin with a Type I singularity. It is entropy unstable by [ CM12 ] , Theorem 0.12, which applies to this compact embedded non-spherical hypersurface. No exact entropy value or global uniqueness assertion is supplied here. Berchenko–Kogan's numerical calculation estimates its entropy as approximately $1.85122$ ( [ CatBerchenkoKogan2021 ] , Section 5, PDF pp. 10–12). This estimate has no certified error enclosure; Section 6, Question 6.3, leaves rigorous error bounds open. The proved bound for the separately constructed variational torus is recorded in Example 2.9.1 . The interactive figure revolves a numerically closed solution of this ODE; its caption records the shooting residual. The profile is not circular. The variational torus in [ CatDLN2018 ] , Theorem 2, is a separate existence construction; that survey does not identify it with Angenent's torus.

title: 2.6 Drugan's immersed shrinking spheres
text: [ CatDrugan2015 ] , Theorem 1.1, p. 3139, proves the existence of a nonembedded immersed $S^2$ self-shrinker in $\mathbb R^3$. [ CatDLN2018 ] , Theorem 3, PDF pp. 14–15, gives the corresponding existence statement for $S^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\geq 2$. Example 2.6.1 (Drugan's immersed shrinking spheres) . FE38A115C52C For each $n\geq 2$, there is a smooth rotational immersion $X:S^ n\to \mathbb R^{n+1}$ satisfying $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$ whose image is not embedded. The associated immersed flow is $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$, $-\infty <t<0$. In the three-dimensional construction, a graphical piece of the profile, written as axial height $z=\gamma (r)$ for $r>0$, solves \[  \frac{\gamma ''}{1+(\gamma ')^2} =\left(\frac r2-\frac1r\right)\gamma '-\frac\gamma 2.  \] This is equation (1.2) of [ CatDrugan2015 ] , p. 3140; the paper's radial variable $x$ is denoted here by $r$. Equation (1.3) describes the same curve as a radius depending on height. Shooting and continuation through profile turning points produce the closed immersed sphere; a single graphical piece does not describe the whole surface. The parameter domain is the compact sphere, so the induced metric is complete and the immersion is proper. The image has self-intersections and is not the round sphere. The construction has rotational symmetry and reflection symmetry across a hyperplane perpendicular to the rotation axis. It has no ends. The homothetic flow contracts to the origin with Type I curvature growth. The cited existence argument supplies neither an elementary parametrization nor uniqueness or an exact entropy value. Embedded classification and embedded stability theorems cannot be applied to this immersion by dropping their embeddedness hypothesis. Numerical picture. The picture computes the rotational shooting construction in [ CatDrugan2015 ] , Sections 2–5, and can be compared with Figure 1 on p. 3141. It shows the two-dimensional immersed sphere in $\mathbb R^3$, not a higher-dimensional projection. Let $s$ be arc length along the meridian and let $\theta $ be its tangent angle measured from the positive radial direction. Substituting $\gamma '=\tan \theta $ into the graph equation gives \[  \frac{dr}{ds}=\cos \theta ,\qquad \frac{dz}{ds}=\sin \theta ,\qquad \frac{d\theta }{ds} =\left(\frac r2-\frac1r\right)\sin \theta -\frac z2\cos \theta .  \] This system continues through the vertical tangents where the graph equation becomes unsuitable for numerical integration. At the upper pole $(r,z)=(0,b)$, smoothness requires $\theta =0$. The even expansion from the graph equation, consistent with Section 6 of the paper, is \[  z(r)=b-\frac b8r^2-\frac{b(b^2+4)}{1024}r^4+O(r^6).  \] We start at $r=10^{-4}$ using this expansion and shoot in $b$ until $z=0$ at the second radial turning point, where $\theta =-3\pi /2$. This is the orthogonal reflection condition in Section 5, pp. 3154–3155. The computation gives \[  b\simeq 0.39345656,\qquad r_{\mathrm{reflection}}\simeq 0.83684239.  \] Reflection across $z=0$, with the order of traversal reversed, completes the meridian from $(0,b)$ to $(0,-b)$. Revolving it gives \[  X(s,\varphi )=(r(s)\cos \varphi ,r(s)\sin \varphi ,z(s)), \qquad 0\leq \varphi <2\pi ,  \] with the angular circles collapsed at the two poles. This is a numerical parametrization at time $t=-1$; the corresponding flow is $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$ for $t<0$. The meridian view shows the self-intersections directly. The revolution angle control reveals interior sheets by removing angular sectors; the resulting cut edges are display boundaries, not boundaries of the immersed sphere. The two colors distinguish the shot half from its reflected continuation. The shooting height residual is below $10^{-10}$ before rounding the exported mesh. Halving the initial radius and maximum step and tightening the integration tolerances changes the computed pole height and reflection radius by less than $10^{-9}$. These are floating-point convergence diagnostics, not certified error bounds. In particular, numerical shooting does not prove existence, uniqueness, or that this root is the supremum used in Drugan's proof.

section: 2.22 The Clifford shrinking torus in four-space
text: We follow the supplied June 2020 version of [ CatELS2020 ] ; its Sections 2, 4 and 5 distinguish exact geometry, Hamiltonian stability, flow instability and local rigidity. Example 2.22.1 (The Clifford shrinking torus in four-space) . 635FBEF68A7E The exact normalized immersion is \[  X(\theta _1,\theta _2)=\sqrt2 (\cos \theta _1,\sin \theta _1,\cos \theta _2,\sin \theta _2), \qquad (\theta _1,\theta _2)\in (\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)^2.  \] It lies in $\mathbb R^4=\mathbb C^2$, and $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$ gives a smooth flow for $t<0$. This is a compact embedded Lagrangian torus of dimension two and codimension two, complete and proper. It is minimal in $S^3(2)$ and has the product rotation symmetry $U(1)\times U(1)$. The induced metric is $2(d\theta _1^2+d\theta _2^2)$; it is intrinsically flat, has area $8\pi ^2$, $|\vec H|=1$, and $\vec H=-X/2$. Its entropy is exactly $2\pi /e$ ( [ CatELS2020 ] , Section 2 and Lemma 2.4, PDF pp. 3–6). It is $F$-unstable under Lagrangian variations but $F$-stable under Hamiltonian variations after accounting for translations. It is locally volume minimizing under Hamiltonian variations (Lemmas 4.1–4.2 and Theorem 4.3, PDF p. 13). Nevertheless it is not a local entropy minimum, even within Hamiltonian variations. For every $\varepsilon >0$ and $k\in \mathbb N$ there is a compact embedded Lagrangian torus Hamiltonian isotopic and $\varepsilon $-close in $C^ k$ whose first finite-time singularity has a blow-up outside the $U(2)$-orbit of the Clifford torus (Corollary 4.8 and Theorem 4.9, PDF p. 16). A compact embedded two-dimensional self-shrinker in $\mathbb C^2$ sufficiently $C^{2,\alpha }$-close, for $0<\alpha <1$, is the Clifford torus up to translation, dilation and rotation (Theorem 5.7, PDF p. 29). This is a local rigidity statement. The interactive picture rotates the second and fourth coordinates in $\mathbb R^4$ and then projects onto the first three coordinates. Apparent intersections in a projection do not mean that the original torus is immersed nonembedded.

title: 2.23 Products of closed shrinking curves
text: [ CatSmoczyk2005 ] , equation (1.4), p. 2984, describes these Lagrangian products. That paper uses $\vec H=-X^\perp $; spatial dilation by $\sqrt2$ converts its examples to the convention used here. Example 2.23.1 (Products of closed shrinking curves) . AD717A30B415 Let $m\geq 2$ and let each $\gamma _ j:S^1\to \mathbb R^2$ be a normalized closed Abresch–Langer shrinker, including the round circle if desired. Then \[  X(u_1,\ldots ,u_ m) =(\gamma _1(u_1),\ldots ,\gamma _ m(u_ m))\in \mathbb R^{2m}, \qquad (u_1,\ldots ,u_ m)\in (S^1)^ m  \] satisfies $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$ for $t<0$. The product formula is exact, but any noncircular factor still requires the curvature ODE and closing condition. The domain is the compact $m$-torus. These are complete proper immersions of dimension and codimension $m$, Lagrangian in $\mathbb C^ m$, with flat normal bundle and nowhere vanishing mean-curvature vector. The product metric is intrinsically flat. A product is embedded when every factor is an embedded circle. A noncircular factor has self-intersections, and so does the product immersion. Multiple covers must not be treated as embeddings. Unless all factor images are circles, the image is not contained in a sphere. The all-circle product in $\mathbb R^4$ is the Clifford torus described separately above. These compact products have no ends and finite entropy. The centered Gaussian integral factors, so $\lambda (\gamma _1\times \cdots \times \gamma _ m)=\prod _ j\lambda (\gamma _ j)$, with the immersion multiplicity counted. They have a Type I homothetic extinction at the origin. No general stability or uniqueness claim for this family is taken from the cited product construction. The figure displays the planar factors and identifies the ambient dimension of their product.

title: 2.24 Higher-codimension spherical shrinkers
text: Minimal submanifolds of a round sphere give Euclidean self-shrinkers. This correspondence, and a converse with hypotheses, appear in [ CatSmoczyk2005 ] , p. 2985 and Theorem 1.1. We use the $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$ scaling. Example 2.24.1 (Higher-codimension spherical shrinkers) . 45597E4891F4 Let $n\geq 2$, $N\geq n+2$, and let $F:M^ n\to S^{N-1}(\sqrt{2n})$ be a smooth compact minimal immersion. Viewed in $\mathbb R^ N$, it satisfies \[  \vec H=-\frac12F, \qquad F_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, F,\quad -\infty <t<0.  \] An explicit family is obtained for integers $p,q\geq 1$, $n=p+q$, by \[  F(u,v)=(\sqrt{2p}\, u,\sqrt{2q}\, v), \quad (u,v)\in S^ p(1)\times S^ q(1), \quad N=p+q+2.  \] To avoid repeating the Clifford torus entry, one may take $p+q\geq 3$ in this explicit family. For a general compact minimal immersion, the resulting shrinker is complete and proper; it is embedded when the original immersion is embedded. Topology, symmetry and further curvature properties depend on the chosen minimal submanifold and are not fixed by this construction. Its mean-curvature vector has constant length $\sqrt{n/2}$, and the principal normal $\vec H/|\vec H|$ is parallel in the normal bundle. Conversely, a compact self-shrinker of dimension $n\geq 2$ is spherical if and only if its mean-curvature vector is nowhere zero and its principal normal is parallel (Smoczyk's Theorem 1.1). The displayed product family is compact embedded of Euclidean codimension two, with topology $S^ p\times S^ q$ and $O(p+1)\times O(q+1)$ symmetry. It has $|A|^2=1$ and is minimal inside $S^{n+1}(\sqrt{2n})$; these identities follow directly from its two round factors. For these explicit products, Gaussian factorization gives $\lambda (S^ p(\sqrt{2p})\times S^ q(\sqrt{2q}))=\lambda (S^ p(\sqrt{2p}))\lambda (S^ q(\sqrt{2q}))$. For a general compact minimal immersion $M^ n\subset S^{N-1}(\sqrt{2n})$, $F_{0,1}(M)=(4\pi )^{-n/2}e^{-n/2}\operatorname {Area}(M)$ by the constant radius. The explicit spherical products are locally rigid: for fixed $p,q\geq 1$ and $0<\alpha <1$, a normalized shrinker in $\mathbb R^ N$, $N\geq p+q+2$, sufficiently close in $C^{2,\alpha }$ to the product is an ambient rotation of it. This is [ CatSunZhu2025 ] , Theorems 1.1–1.2, PDF p. 1. It is a local statement with center and scale fixed, not global uniqueness. The formula determines the product geometry exactly. The figure is a factor diagram with the full ambient dimension stated.

section: 2.7 Møller closed shrinkers of large even genus
text: Møller's construction is stated in [ CatMoller2014 ] , Theorem 1, and summarized in the supplied [ CatDLN2018 ] , Section 3.3, PDF pp. 10–11. Example 2.7.1 (Møller closed shrinkers of large even genus) . A105C87CB202 There is an integer $g_0$ such that for every even $g\geq g_0$ there exists a compact smooth embedded orientable surface $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$ satisfying $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$. Its flow is $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g$, $t<0$. This is an existence construction by desingularization, not an explicit formula and not an existence assertion for every positive genus. Each surface is complete and proper, has no ends, and is invariant under a dihedral group of order $2g$. Along the constructed family as $g\to \infty $, the surfaces converge in Hausdorff distance to the union of a round shrinking sphere and a rotational shrinking torus. Convergence is locally smooth away from their two intersection circles ( [ CatMoller2014 ] , pp. 1–2). The limiting union is singular and is not one of the smooth members. These surfaces are not mean convex and are entropy unstable: apply [ CM12 ] , Theorems 0.17 and 0.12, to the compact embedded non-spherical surfaces. Their homothetic flows have Type I extinction at the origin. The cited construction supplies no exact coordinates or exact entropy value and makes no uniqueness assertion for a specified genus. The illustration follows Figures 1–2 of [ CatMoller2014 ] : a sphere of radius $2$ intersects a non-circular rotational shrinking torus along two circles. In cylindrical coordinates $(r,\theta ,z)$, the displayed numerical torus meets the sphere near $r=1.783$, $z=\pm 0.906$, consistent with Proposition 2.1. These are numerical coordinates, not exact formulas. Rotation, a quarter cutaway, and a meridian view expose both sheets and the circles where the desingularization takes place. The removed sector is only a viewing aid. As in the paper's Figure 1, this is the singular configuration before handle insertion, not a computed smooth surface $\Sigma _ g$. The second illustration shows how the two intersection circles can be replaced by handles, using gluing schematics of genera $8$, $16$, and $24$. Their mesh topology is checked, but these models do not solve the self-shrinker equation and are not certified approximations to $\Sigma _ g$. The chosen genera illustrate the topology; the cited theorem does not give an explicit $g_0$ that would establish these particular values as members of its constructed family.

title: 2.8 Kapouleas–Kleene–Møller shrinkers with one end
text: The original construction is [ CatKKM2018 ] , Theorem 1.1, arXiv version 3, PDF p. 2. It is among the examples cited in the introduction of [ CatSunWang2020 ] . Example 2.8.1 (Kapouleas–Kleene–Møller shrinkers with one end) . A515DF7C7C60 There is an integer $g_0$ such that for every integer $g\geq g_0$ there exists a smooth complete embedded orientable self-shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$, with \[  \vec H=-\frac12X^\perp ,\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g,\quad -\infty <t<0.  \] The construction desingularizes the intersection circle of a plane through the origin and $S^2(2)$. title: 2.9 Drugan–Nguyen variational shrinking tori
text: This is the variational construction in [ CatDruganNguyen2018 ] , Theorem 1, arXiv version 1, PDF p. 1. Its identification with the torus obtained by Angenent's shooting construction is not established in this source. The separate entry records the proved Gaussian-area bound, without claiming that the two constructions give distinct surfaces. Example 2.9.1 (Drugan–Nguyen variational shrinking tori) . 9F3C76F8391F For every integer $n\geq 2$, the weighted half-plane $\{ (r,x):r>0\} $ with metric \[  g_ n=r^{2(n-1)}e^{-(r^2+x^2)/2}(dr^2+dx^2)  \] contains a simple closed geodesic $\gamma _ n=(r,x)$ whose weighted length satisfies \[  L_{g_ n}(\gamma _ n)<2\int _0^\infty s^{n-1}e^{-s^2/4}\, ds.  \] Revolving this curve gives a normalized self-shrinker \[  X(u,\omega )=(r(u)\omega ,x(u)),\qquad (u,\omega )\in S^1\times S^{n-1}(1), \qquad \vec H=-X^\perp /2.  \] The profile is obtained by a variational and modified curve-flow argument, not by a closed formula. The smooth MCF is $\sqrt{-t}\, X$, $t<0$. This is a compact embedded hypersurface of dimension $n$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, with topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$ and rotational $O(n)$ symmetry. It is complete, proper, boundaryless and has no ends. For $n=2$ it is an embedded genus-one torus in $\mathbb R^3$. The rotational Gaussian integral and the length bound give \[  \lambda (\mathcal T_ n)=F_{0,1}(\mathcal T_ n) =(4\pi )^{-n/2}|S^{n-1}(1)|L_{g_ n}(\gamma _ n)<2.  \] Thus this family has a proved entropy upper bound in every stated dimension. The theorem does not provide an exact entropy value. In dimension two, this is the shrinking doughnut $\mathcal T$ used by [ CatChuSun2025 ] , Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 1.7, to produce genus-one singularities and an embedded genus-one shrinker of strictly lower entropy. That conclusion does not identify the lower-entropy model with a particular previously constructed family. The asserted bound is attached to this variationally constructed torus. A numerical value for the Angenent shooting profile is a different type of evidence and does not establish that the profiles coincide. The illustration shows the weighted half-plane construction and a clearly labelled torus topology schematic. Reusing a numerical Angenent mesh as an exact model of this construction would assume the unproved identification.

title: Example 2.9.1 (Drugan–Nguyen variational shrinking tori)
text: Example 2.9.1 (Drugan–Nguyen variational shrinking tori) . 9F3C76F8391F For every integer $n\geq 2$, the weighted half-plane $\{ (r,x):r>0\} $ with metric \[  g_ n=r^{2(n-1)}e^{-(r^2+x^2)/2}(dr^2+dx^2)  \] contains a simple closed geodesic $\gamma _ n=(r,x)$ whose weighted length satisfies \[  L_{g_ n}(\gamma _ n)<2\int _0^\infty s^{n-1}e^{-s^2/4}\, ds.  \] Revolving this curve gives a normalized self-shrinker \[  X(u,\omega )=(r(u)\omega ,x(u)),\qquad (u,\omega )\in S^1\times S^{n-1}(1), \qquad \vec H=-X^\perp /2.  \] The profile is obtained by a variational and modified curve-flow argument, not by a closed formula. The smooth MCF is $\sqrt{-t}\, X$, $t<0$. This is a compact embedded hypersurface of dimension $n$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, with topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$ and rotational $O(n)$ symmetry. It is complete, proper, boundaryless and has no ends. For $n=2$ it is an embedded genus-one torus in $\mathbb R^3$. The rotational Gaussian integral and the length bound give \[  \lambda (\mathcal T_ n)=F_{0,1}(\mathcal T_ n) =(4\pi )^{-n/2}|S^{n-1}(1)|L_{g_ n}(\gamma _ n)<2.  \] Thus this family has a proved entropy upper bound in every stated dimension. The theorem does not provide an exact entropy value. In dimension two, this is the shrinking doughnut $\mathcal T$ used by [ CatChuSun2025 ] , Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 1.7, to produce genus-one singularities and an embedded genus-one shrinker of strictly lower entropy. That conclusion does not identify the lower-entropy model with a particular previously constructed family. The asserted bound is attached to this variationally constructed torus. A numerical value for the Angenent shooting profile is a different type of evidence and does not establish that the profiles coincide. The illustration shows the weighted half-plane construction and a clearly labelled torus topology schematic. Reusing a numerical Angenent mesh as an exact model of this construction would assume the unproved identification.

section: 2.10 Buzano–Nguyen–Schulz shrinkers of every positive genus
text: [ CatBNS2025 ] , Theorems 1.2–1.3, arXiv version 2, PDF p. 2, establish this family by equivariant min-max methods. The family is discussed in [ CatChuSun2025 ] , Remark 1.5. Example 2.10.1 (Buzano–Nguyen–Schulz shrinkers of every positive genus) . 40F2B3444C2E For every integer $g\geq 1$ there exists a complete embedded noncompact self-shrinker $\Theta _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$. The smooth flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, \Theta _ g$ for $t<0$, using $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$. There is no explicit parametrization. These surfaces have dimension two and codimension one, are proper and boundaryless, and have a finite number of annular ends. Properness and the end topology are recorded in Corollary 2.8, PDF p. 8. They have at least one asymptotically conical end. Any additional ends are asymptotically conical or cylindrical. The proved symmetry is invariance under the dihedral group $D_{g+1}$ of order $2(g+1)$, generated by half-turns about $g+1$ horizontal axes. The surface contains these axes and meets the vertical axis orthogonally. Additional reflection symmetry is proposed, rather than proved, in Section 2, PDF pp. 3–4. For all sufficiently large $g$, there is exactly one asymptotically conical end. As $g\to \infty $, $\Theta _ g$ converges as a varifold to the union of the horizontal plane and $S^2(2)$, smoothly locally away from their intersection circle. Theorem 1.3 does not establish exactly one end for every small genus. The normalized Gaussian area satisfies the proved bound \[  1<F_{0,1}(\Theta _ g)\leq 1.02+\frac4e<3.  \] This is Lemmas 2.5–2.6, PDF p. 7: the multiplicity is one and $F_{0,1}(\Theta _ g)$ equals the min-max width. For these normalized complete shrinkers, Gaussian area equals entropy. The numerical simulation for $g=1$ gives Gaussian area approximately $1.7143$ (Section 4, Table 1, PDF p. 15). It is not a certified value for a uniquely identified min-max surface. The source conjectures that $\Theta _1$ has lower entropy than the Angenent torus and Gaussian Morse index five; neither statement is its existence theorem. The relation between the large-genus members and the Kapouleas–Kleene–Møller construction is not proved to be equality. The illustration shows the symmetry and topology schematically; it is not a numerical approximation of a min-max surface.

title: 2.11 Ketover self-shrinking doubled planes
text: The following is [ CatKetover2024 ] , Theorem 1.1, arXiv version 2, PDF pp. 2–3. The construction is variational, with genus determined in Section 6 and the ends analyzed in Section 8. Example 2.11.1 (Ketover self-shrinking doubled planes) . 9E9A8A1CC506 For every integer $g\geq 1$ there exists an embedded self-shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$ such that \[  \lambda (\Sigma _ g)=F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ g)<2, \qquad \lim _{g\to \infty }\lambda (\Sigma _ g)=2.  \] The normalized smooth flow is $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g$, $t<0$. There is no explicit formula for $\Sigma _ g$. The construction gives a smooth complete properly embedded boundaryless surface of dimension two and codimension one. It is invariant under the prismatic group $D_{g+1}\times \mathbb Z_2$, including reflection across the horizontal plane $P=\{ z=0\} $. The group has order $4(g+1)$. For all sufficiently large $g$, the surface is noncompact with exactly two asymptotically conical ends: one in $z>0$ and one in $z<0$, each graphical over the exterior of a disk in $P$. Their cone links converge in $C^0$ to the equator as $g\to \infty $. For these $g$, the topology is a closed orientable genus-$g$ surface with two points removed. For the small-genus members, this theorem does not establish noncompactness or an exact number of ends. Numerical evidence for two ends already at $g=1$ is stated separately in Remark 1.2. As $g\to \infty $, $\Sigma _ g\to 2P$ as varifolds. From every subsequence one can extract a further subsequence and find a radius $r>0$ such that the surfaces are two normal graphs converging smoothly on each compact subset of $P\setminus C_ r$, where $C_ r=\{ (x,y,0):x^2+y^2=r^2\} $. The radius is part of the subsequential conclusion, not a prescribed geometric parameter. For sufficiently large $g$, the level set flow starting from the smooth surface $\Sigma _ g$ fattens (Theorem 1.3, PDF p. 4). The homothetic flow reaches its asymptotic cone at time zero; this statement concerns weak continuation beyond that singular time. Entropy minimization among genus-$g$ shrinkers is conjectural (Remark 1.2). Neither uniqueness nor a particular value below two is claimed. The picture is a labelled doubled-plane and neck-circle schematic, with two conical ends only in the sufficiently large genus regime. A diagram of two sheets is not an exact solved shrinker, and the multiplicity-two plane is a varifold limit rather than a smooth member.

title: 2.12 Closed shrinkers from spherical doubling
text: Example 2.12.1 (Closed shrinkers from spherical doubling) . 826D61792601 For every sufficiently large integer $m$, Kapouleas–McGrath construct a smooth closed embedded surface $S_ m\subset \mathbb R^3$ by doubling the round self-shrinking sphere $S^2(2)$. In the two-latitude subfamily, two nearby sphere sheets are joined by $2m$ small catenoidal bridges, with $m$ bridge sites on each of two latitude circles. The resulting surface satisfies \[  \vec H_{S_ m}=-\frac{X^\perp }{2},\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, S_ m,\quad -\infty <t<0.  \] The formula specifies the evolution after the existence construction; it is not an explicit formula for $S_ m$. The surface has dimension two and codimension one. It is connected, orientable, compact without boundary, smoothly embedded, complete and proper. Its genus is $g=2m-1$, and it has no topological ends. This statement is the specialization $k_\circ =2$ and $\mathbf m=(m)$ of the construction. The threshold for sufficiently large $m$ is not made effective here. It does not supply all small genera. The selected surfaces are invariant under $\mathcal G_ m=D_{2m}\times \mathbb Z_2$, of order $4m$, where $D_{2m}$ denotes a dihedral group of order $2m$. This is an asserted symmetry subgroup, not a classification of the entire isometry group. As $m\to \infty $, the surfaces converge as varifolds to the radius-two sphere with multiplicity two. Each member before the limit is a smooth embedded connected surface; the doubled sphere is the limiting configuration. Since $S_ m$ is a centered shrinker, its entropy equals its normalized Gaussian area. The area inequality in the Gaussian metric $g=e^{-|x|^2/4}g_{\rm Euc}$ gives \[  \lambda (S_ m)=F(S_ m)=\frac1{4\pi }\int _{S_ m}e^{-|x|^2/4}\, d\mathcal H^2 <2F(S^2(2))=\frac8e.  \] This is a rigorous bound obtained from the gluing theorem, not a numerical entropy computation. An individual numerical entropy, the exact Gaussian Morse index, and a uniqueness classification are not recorded by this entry. The spherical input has the required trivial Jacobi kernel, verified directly in Section 10 of the source. This specialization does not rely on the separate theorem on doubling the Angenent torus. See [ CatKapouleasMcGrath2023 ] , arXiv version 4: Theorem 10.5 (PDF page 66), Theorem 9.40 (page 65), Definitions 7.10–7.11 and Remark 7.12 (page 40), and Theorem 5.7 with equation (5.9) (page 30; also Theorem A on page 3). The genus formula is $2g_{S^2}-1+|L|=-1+2m$. The bridge diagram is schematic and does not compute a solution or assert that its displayed number of dots is in the existence range.

title: 2.13 Nguyen's one-ended shrinking saddles
text: Example 2.13.1 (Nguyen's one-ended shrinking saddles) . B28BB2912147 For every sufficiently large integer $m$, Nguyen constructs a smooth complete embedded surface $\widetilde M_ m\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $m-1$, with one asymptotically conical end. The source uses \[  \mathbf H_{\widetilde M_ m}=-\widetilde X^\perp .  \] Thus the catalogue's normalized example is $M_ m=\sqrt{2}\, \widetilde M_ m$, which satisfies $\mathbf H=-X^\perp /2$, and its flow is $M_ m(t)=\sqrt{-t}\, M_ m$ for $t<0$. The construction replaces the intersection circle of a sphere and a plane by a bent, scaled singly periodic Scherk surface, then solves the nonlinear shrinker equation by a perturbation argument. In the catalogue normalization the input sphere has radius $2$. This is an existence construction, with no closed parametrization of the completed shrinker. Its proved properties and construction data include the following. The surface has dimension two and codimension one. It is connected, orientable, noncompact, proper, and without boundary. Outside a compact set it is a graph over the exterior of a planar disk. Consequently it has one topological end; the asymptotic cone is not an assertion that the end is planar. The $m$ periods of the Scherk piece produce genus $m-1$. The existence theorem requires $m$ sufficiently large and does not establish the small-$m$ cases. The surface is invariant under a half-turn about the $x$-axis and under reflections in vertical planes making angles $\pi /(2m)+j\pi /m$, $j\in \mathbb Z$, with that axis. These are finite symmetries, not full rotational symmetry. As $m\to \infty $, the source proves convergence to the spherical input on compact subsets of the upper half-ball in Theorem 1(iv), and convergence to the singly periodic Scherk model after translating and rescaling the joining region in Theorem 1(vi). These limits describe different spatial scales. The conical graphical end gives quadratic area growth and finite entropy. In the stated normalization $F_{0,1}(M_ m)=\lambda (M_ m)$; no scalar entropy value or uniform numerical bound is recorded here. The theorem does not give a global uniqueness or stability classification. Source: [ CatNguyenShrinker2014 ] , Theorem 1 and its preceding topology paragraph, PDF p. 2; the construction of the outer graphical piece and Proposition 14, PDF p. 13; Definition 21, PDF p. 20; the final fixed-point argument, PDF pp. 24–25. This is another sphere–plane desingularization construction beside Example 2.8.1 ; no identification or noncongruence between the two families is asserted. The illustration shows construction inputs and a symbolic joining region, not a solved shrinker.

title: 2.25 Angenent torus cylinders
text: Example 2.25.1 (Angenent torus cylinders) . FA65887C28F1 Let $T^2\subset \mathbb R^3$ be a normalized embedded Angenent shrinking torus as in Example 2.5.1 . For every integer $k\geq 1$, its Euclidean product \[  \Sigma _ k=T^2\times \mathbb R^ k\subset \mathbb R^{k+3}  \] is a smooth embedded shrinker of dimension $k+2$ and codimension one. If $X_ T(p)$ parametrizes the torus, the exact product and flow formulas are \[  X(p,z)=(X_ T(p),z),\qquad \Sigma _ k(t)=\sqrt{-t}\, T^2\times \mathbb R^ k,\quad t<0.  \] The torus factor itself is specified by its closed weighted geodesic or rotational ODE, not by a closed elementary formula. Since the Euclidean factor is tangent to the product, \[  \mathbf H_{\Sigma _ k}=(\mathbf H_ T,0)=-\tfrac 12(X_ T^\perp ,0) =-\tfrac 12X^\perp .  \] This verifies the product construction directly. Each product is connected, complete, proper, noncompact, and without boundary, with topology $T^2\times \mathbb R^ k$. It has two topological ends when $k=1$ and one when $k\geq 2$. Its intrinsic dimension is at least three, so a surface genus is not assigned; genus one describes the torus factor only. The product inherits the torus's axial rotational symmetry and is invariant under translations and orthogonal transformations in the Euclidean factor. The two ends of $\Sigma _1\subset \mathbb R^4$ have the fixed torus as cross-section. Gaussian integration in the Euclidean factor gives, for $a\in \mathbb R^3$, $b\in \mathbb R^ k$, and $\tau >0$, \[  F_{(a,b),\tau }(\Sigma _ k)=F_{a,\tau }(T^2),\qquad \lambda (\Sigma _ k)=\lambda (T^2)=F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ k).  \] Indeed, the extra factor is $(4\pi \tau )^{-k/2}\int _{\mathbb R^ k}e^{-|z-b|^2/(4\tau )}\, dz=1$. Thus the numerical estimate $1.85122$ for the torus also estimates these products, with the same lack of a certified error enclosure; the product identity itself is exact. As Euclidean products of a closed nonflat embedded shrinker, these examples fall within the realization theorem of [ CatCLSZ2026 ] , Theorem 1.2, PDF p. 2: each can occur with multiplicity one as a first-singularity tangent flow of a closed embedded hypersurface in the corresponding Euclidean space. The theorem does not assert that the initial closed hypersurface is this noncompact product. The factor is constructed in [ CatAngenent1992 ] ; the numerical entropy estimate is [ CatBerchenkoKogan2021 ] , Section 5, with its error-bound limitation in Section 6. The interactive picture shows only three $z$-slices of $\Sigma _1$ after projection from $\mathbb R^4$ to $\mathbb R^3$. It uses the catalogue's numerical torus mesh. Apparent intersections are projection artifacts; the three slices do not represent three components or the entire three-dimensional hypersurface.

title: 2.14 Ilmanen–White two-ended shrinkers
text: Example 2.14.1 (Ilmanen–White two-ended shrinkers) . 4522A41972E4 For every integer $h\geq 2$, Ilmanen–White construct a smooth complete properly embedded self-shrinking surface $\Sigma _ h\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $h$ with exactly two ends. In their notation the initial wheel has genus $g=h+1$ and its tangent shrinker has genus $g-1$. The normalized flow is \[  \vec H=-X^\perp /2,\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ h,\quad t<0.  \] There is no explicit formula: $\Sigma _ h$ is obtained as a tangent flow of a critical wheel. This is a connected orientable noncompact surface, of dimension two and codimension one, with topology a closed genus-$h$ surface with two punctures. Both ends are smoothly asymptotically conical. The part above $P=\{ z=0\} $ is a graph over the unbounded component of $P\setminus \Sigma _ h$; the lower part is its reflection. The intersection with $P$ consists of $h+1$ disjoint smooth closed curves. Its symmetries include reflection in $P$, reflections in the vertical planes at angles $j\pi /(h+1)$, and rotation through $2\pi /(h+1)$ about the vertical axis. The two cone links lie on opposite sides of the equator. The authors construct a compact embedded initial surface of genus $h+1$ whose first singular time has exactly one singular point and this multiplicity-one tangent shrinker. Corollary 4.11 gives uniqueness of the tangent flow at that point, not uniqueness of all shrinkers with these topological data. As $h\to \infty $, the shrinkers converge as varifolds to $2P$. After passage to a subsequence, convergence is smooth with multiplicity two away from one circle in $P$. For sufficiently large $h$, the initial compact wheel fattens immediately after its first singular time. No effective genus threshold for fattening is given. section: 2.15 Shao–Zou shrinkers with any prescribed number of ends
text: Example 2.15.1 (Shao–Zou plane stackings) . 4BFAC8529BEA Fix an integer $k\geq 2$. For every sufficiently large integer $m$, with the threshold allowed to depend on $k$, Shao–Zou construct an embedded self-shrinker $\Sigma _{k,m}\subset \mathbb R^3$ with \[  \operatorname {genus}(\Sigma _{k,m})=(k-1)(m-1),\qquad \# \operatorname {ends}(\Sigma _{k,m})=k, \qquad \vec H=-X^\perp /2.  \] Their parameter is $J=(k-1)/2$. The smooth flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _{k,m}$ for $t<0$. The surface is obtained by elliptic gluing, rather than an explicit parametrization. The construction stacks $k$ perturbations of the horizontal plane and connects each consecutive pair by $m$ catenoidal bridges. Thus there are $(k-1)m$ bridges in total, placed on alternating equally spaced neck configurations around a circle. The compact core and graphical ends give a connected, orientable, complete, proper, boundaryless noncompact surface. Each of the $k$ annular ends is asymptotic to a cone. Theorem 8.1 gives the leading cone slopes in terms of the solved bridge parameters with error estimates; these asymptotic expressions are not formulas for the whole shrinker. For even $k$, the asserted symmetry is the $m$-gonal prism group $D_{mh}$; for odd $k$, it is the $m$-gonal antiprism group $D_{md}$. Both have order $4m$. Horizontal reflection is a symmetry in the even-$k$ case and is not an element of the stated antiprism group in the odd-$k$ case. For fixed $k$ and $m\to \infty $, $\Sigma _{k,m}$ converges as a varifold to the horizontal plane with multiplicity $k$. Each surface before the limit is embedded with multiplicity one. The limiting plane is not a smooth member of the positive-genus family. Conical ends imply quadratic area growth and finite entropy, and $F_{0,1}(\Sigma _{k,m})=\lambda (\Sigma _{k,m})$. No exact value or numerical entropy upper bound is asserted here. A local varifold limit alone is not used to assign a numerical entropy limit. The source expects its $k=2$ and $k=3$ examples to agree with earlier doubled- and tripled-plane constructions when the parameters overlap, but it does not prove those identifications. It supplies no uniqueness or exact Morse-index classification. See [ CatShaoZou2025 ] , version 1: the introductory theorem (PDF p. 2), Definition 2.28 and Remark 2.29 (p. 7), and Theorem 8.1 (pp. 31–32). In particular, this gives examples with four or more ends, beyond the one-, two-, and three-ended constructions already listed. The bridge-and-sheet illustration is schematic; its small displayed bridge count is not asserted to meet the large-$m$ hypothesis.

title: 2.16 Flow-generated Platonic and polygonal shrinkers
text: Example 2.16.1 (Hoffman–Martin–White ray-avoiding shrinkers) . A455BCCC51D0 Let $Q\subset \mathbb R^3$ be the union of rays from the origin through either the face centers of a regular Platonic solid or the vertices of a regular horizontal $n$-gon, $n\geq 3$. If $q$ is the number of rays, Hoffman–Martin–White construct a smooth embedded shrinker $\Sigma _ Q$ of genus $q-1$ such that \[  \Sigma _ Q\cap Q=\varnothing ,\qquad \vec H_{\Sigma _ Q}=-X^\perp /2.  \] The associated smooth flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ Q$, $t<0$. This is a construction through singularities of mean curvature flow, not an explicit formula. The surface has dimension two and codimension one, is complete, proper, orientable and without boundary, and has all symmetries of $Q$. The genera are $3,5,7,11,19$ for the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron respectively. For the regular $n$-gon the genus is $n-1$. It occurs with multiplicity one as a tangent shrinker of an initially compact, smoothly embedded surface in $\mathbb R^3\setminus Q$. This realization statement is part of the construction, rather than an identification with Ketover's min-max surface. The theorem does not determine compactness or the number and types of ends for the Platonic examples or the small-$n$ polygonal examples. The discussion after the theorem states that the polygonal examples are noncompact for sufficiently large $n$ and converge to a multiplicity-two plane as $n\to \infty $; it does not give an exact end count there. Each example has finite entropy as a tangent shrinker of a compact initial flow, and $\lambda (\Sigma _ Q)=F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ Q)$. No numerical entropy bound or exact value is recorded here. No uniqueness or equality with the corresponding Ketover or Ilmanen–White constructions is asserted. See [ CatHMW2026 ] , version 3: Theorem 12 and its discussion (PDF pp. 8–9), with the multiplicity-one tangent-flow convention on p. 4. The compact numerical pictures mentioned in the paper do not establish compactness of the members selected by the theorem. The illustration depicts the excluded rays and symmetry data only.

title: 2.17 Flow-generated sphere–plane shrinkers
text: Example 2.17.1 (Hoffman–Martin–White sphere–plane family) . 45B364E949D5 Write $d_1=\sqrt{2\pi /e}$ and $d_2=4/e$. For every integer $g\geq 1$ and every fixed \[  1+d_2<\delta <1+d_1,  \] Hoffman–Martin–White construct a smooth embedded shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$ with $\lambda (\Sigma _ g)<\delta $. They produce it as a tangent shrinker of an intrinsically flowing compact surface in $S^2\times \mathbb R$; the tangent shrinker itself is Euclidean. It satisfies $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, with homothetic flow $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g$ for $t<0$. No explicit parametrization is known from this construction. This is a connected, orientable, complete, properly embedded surface of dimension two and codimension one. It contains the union $Q_ g$ of $g+1$ horizontal lines through the origin at angles $j\pi /(g+1)$, and $\Sigma _ g\cap \{ z=0\} =Q_ g$. In particular it is noncompact. Its complement of the horizontal plane has genus zero. The symmetry group $G_ g$ used here is generated by reflection in vertical planes at angles $(2j+1)\pi /(2(g+1))$, rotations about the vertical axis through $2\pi /(g+1)$, and half-turns about the lines in $Q_ g$. This is the Costa–Hoffman–Meeks symmetry group specified in Section 5. For all sufficiently large $g$, $\Sigma _ g$ has exactly one asymptotically conical end. For small $g$, the theorem does not specify an exact number of ends. For a fixed admissible $\delta $, as $g\to \infty $ the surfaces converge to $\{ z=0\} \cup S^2(2)$, smoothly with multiplicity one away from the equatorial intersection circle. The normalized Gaussian area equals entropy and obeys \[  F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ g)=\lambda (\Sigma _ g)<\delta <1+\sqrt{2\pi /e}<3.  \] The choice of $\delta $ is part of the existence statement; it does not assign an exact entropy to a fixed uniquely determined member. No identification with the Buzano–Nguyen–Schulz min-max examples or the Kapouleas–Kleene–Moller and Nguyen gluing examples is proved. The shared topology and limiting configuration do not establish that they coincide or are distinct. See [ CatHMW2026 ] , version 3: Section 5 (PDF pp. 16–17), Theorems 40–42 (pp. 26–31), Section 9 (p. 40), and Lemma 64 (pp. 45–46). title: 2.18 Flow-generated three-ended shrinkers
text: Example 2.18.1 (Hoffman–Martin–White three-ended family) . 5CED6ED3B586 For every sufficiently large integer $g$, Hoffman–Martin–White construct a smooth embedded shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ with genus $2g$ and exactly three ends. It has the normalization and smooth evolution \[  \vec H=-X^\perp /2,\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g,\quad t<0.  \] The construction obtains the surface as a multiplicity-one tangent shrinker of a flow whose initial surface is compact and embedded in $S^2\times \mathbb R$ with its product metric. The shrinker lives in the Euclidean tangent space. There is no explicit parametrization. It is a connected, orientable, complete, proper noncompact surface of dimension two and codimension one. Its topology is a closed genus-$2g$ surface with three punctures; the three ends are annular and asymptotically conical. It has the group $G_ g$ and the union of lines $Q_ g$ specified in Example 2.17.1 . In particular, $\Sigma _ g\cap \{ z=0\} =Q_ g$ and $\Sigma _ g\setminus \{ z=0\} $ has genus zero. These are the symmetries of the genus-$g$ Costa–Hoffman–Meeks minimal surface, but the shrinker has genus $2g$. As $g\to \infty $, the surfaces converge to the horizontal plane with multiplicity three. After passage to a subsequence, convergence is smooth away from one circle in that plane. The circle is part of the limiting analysis, not an independently prescribed radius. title: 2.19 Ketover shrinkers with Platonic symmetry
text: [ CatKetover2016 ] , Theorem 0.1, constructs five families by equivariant Gaussian min-max. The compact doubled solids used in the sweepout describe the genus and symmetry of the construction; compactness of the limiting shrinker is not proved. Example 2.19.1 (Ketover shrinkers with Platonic symmetry) . AE0CC89EB3E2 There are smooth connected embedded self-shrinking surfaces $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^3$ with the following pairs of genus and rotational symmetry group: \[  (g,G)=(3,T_{12}),\quad (5,O_{24}),\quad (7,O_{24}), \quad (11,I_{60}),\quad (19,I_{60}).  \] Here the subscripts give the orders of the tetrahedral, octahedral, and icosahedral rotation groups. The normalization is $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$. No explicit parametrization is supplied. The sweepout joins two spherical sheets by one neck for each face of a tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, or icosahedron, respectively. The numbers of necks are $4,6,8,12,20$; the first neck connects the components, so the genus is one less than this number. This is a construction description, not an exact metric model. The min-max limit is multiplicity one. It is complete and proper, has no boundary, and retains the stated genus and symmetry. The construction controls the genus but does not determine compactness, the number of ends, or end asymptotics. In particular, a compact picture suggested by numerical work must not be used to assign zero ends to these proved examples. The proof gives a useful strict Gaussian-area bound: \[  \frac4e < F_{0,1}(\Sigma )=\lambda (\Sigma )<\frac8e.  \] For the doubled cube, the first equivariant width is $4/e$, the second is strictly below twice the first by Lemma 2.4, and the equality of the two widths is excluded in Remark 2.7. Remark 2.5 gives the same construction for the other four symmetry types. These are bounds, not computed entropy values. No uniqueness or stability classification is asserted. The two-parameter equivariant construction alone does not give an index bound for unrestricted variations. Later constructions with similar symmetries need not be different surfaces, and no identification is assumed here. section: 2.20 Sun–Wang–Zhou shrinkers of arbitrarily large entropy
text: The Gaussian-width construction of [ CatSunWangZhou2024 ] produces shrinkers whose entropy is unbounded, in contrast with the uniform upper bounds for several gluing and low-parameter min-max families. Example 2.20.1 (Sun–Wang–Zhou Gaussian-width shrinkers) . 0177A2718D72 For every $2\leq n\leq 6$ there is a sequence of smooth, connected, embedded self-shrinking hypersurfaces $\Sigma _ k^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$. They are normalized by $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, with associated smooth flows $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ k$ for $t<0$. The construction is variational and does not give explicit parametrizations. Each shrinker is complete, proper, boundaryless, and has finite entropy. The construction is a multiplicity-one limit of free-boundary min-max hypersurfaces in exhausting balls with metrics approaching the Gaussian metric. The final shrinker has no free boundary. Write $G_ n=(4\pi )^{-1}e^{-|x|^2/(2n)}g_{\mathrm{Euc}}$ and let $\omega _ k(\mathbb R^{n+1},G_ n)$ be its Gaussian $k$-width, defined by exhaustion. Then \[  F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ k)=\lambda (\Sigma _ k) =\omega _ k(\mathbb R^{n+1},G_ n),\qquad \lambda (\Sigma _ k)\asymp k^{1/(n+1)}.  \] The growth statement means comparison up to positive constants depending on $n$, and in particular $\lambda (\Sigma _ k)\to \infty $. It is not a closed formula for an individual width or a plotted list of computed values. The unbounded entropies ensure infinitely many different examples, without requiring consecutive widths to be strictly different. section: 2.21 Chu–Sun genus-one shrinkers below the shrinking doughnut
text: The flow construction in [ CatChuSun2025 ] gives an embedded genus-one shrinker with strictly less entropy than the Drugan–Nguyen shrinking doughnut. It does not identify the resulting surface with any particular previously constructed example. Example 2.21.1 (Chu–Sun lower-entropy genus-one shrinkers) . AE7721D6799F Let $\mathcal T\subset \mathbb R^3$ be the rotationally symmetric compact genus-one shrinker constructed by Drugan–Nguyen (Example 2.9.1 ). There is a smooth embedded genus-one shrinker $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^3$ satisfying \[  F_{0,1}(\Sigma )=\lambda (\Sigma ) <\lambda (\mathcal T)<2.  \] It has dimension two and codimension one, is normalized by $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and yields the smooth self-similar flow $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$. The surface is a multiplicity-one tangent-flow model at a genus-one singularity of an ancient level-set flow which is asymptotic, after rescaling as $t\to -\infty $, to $\mathcal T$. The ancient flow is allowed to pass through cylindrical and spherical singularities before the genus-one singularity. Thus the theorem does not assert that this is the first singularity of a smooth ancient flow. The resulting shrinker is complete, proper, and boundaryless. Its compactness, end count, end asymptotics, and symmetry are not determined by this existence statement. No explicit parametrization, exact entropy value, or numerical shape is supplied. Strictly smaller entropy rules out congruence with the chosen shrinking doughnut $\mathcal T$. It does not prove that $\Sigma $ differs from the Buzano–Nguyen–Schulz genus-one example. Remark 1.5 discusses that example and its numerical evidence, without proving the identification. It also does not identify $\mathcal T$ with Angenent's shooting torus. For a shrinker minimizing entropy among all embedded genus-one shrinkers, Theorem 1.4 gives a further alternative: it is noncompact or has Gaussian Morse index exactly $5$. This statement applies to an entropy minimizer, not to every shrinker obtained by the interpolation construction. No uniqueness is asserted. Sources: [ CatChuSun2025 ] , Theorems 1.4 and 1.6, Remark 1.5 and Corollary 1.7, arXiv version 3, PDF pp. 3–4; proofs in Sections 5.2–5.5, pp. 33–34. The diagram records the flow construction and strict entropy drop; the final genus-one shrinker is left abstract because its compactness and ends are not specified.

title: 3.1 The grim reaper and its cylinders

section: 3.1 The grim reaper and its cylinders
text: Example 3.1.1 (The grim reaper and its cylinders) . 3B1939BC4D74 For unit upward translation, an exact parametrization in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is \[  X(x,y,t)=(x,y,-\log \cos x+t),\qquad |x|<\pi /2,\quad y\in \mathbb R^{n-1},\quad t\in \mathbb R.  \] For $n=1$ omit $y$. More generally the planar curve of speed $c>0$ has height $-c^{-1}\log \cos (cx)+ct$, on $|x|<\pi /(2c)$. The curve and all its Euclidean products are complete, properly embedded, noncompact, and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. Their motion is eternal. At unit speed the curve has curvature magnitude $\cos x$ and total curvature $\pi $. Its two ends have the vertical asymptotes $x=\pm \pi /2$. The product is invariant under translations in its $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ factor. For $n\geq 2$ its second fundamental form has rank one; in $\mathbb R^3$ its Gauss curvature is zero, so it is not strictly convex. As a translating graph it is stable for compactly supported variations of the translator weighted area. This is weighted stability, not a claim about stability for unweighted Euclidean area. The supplied notes [ CatHIMWNotes19 ] , Example 1.6, PDF page 4, use downward translation; the displayed surface is its reflection in a horizontal plane. Graphical weighted minimality is discussed in [ CatHIMWGraphical18 ] , Section 2, PDF page 5.

title: 3.2 Tilted grim-reaper cylinders
text: Example 3.2.1 (Tilted grim-reaper cylinders) . 56A3E33A9D04 Let $a\in \mathbb R$ and $A=1+a^2$. An exact unit-speed upward translator in $\mathbb R^3$ is \[  X(x,y,t)=\left(x,y,-A\log \cos (x/\sqrt A)+ay+t\right),\quad |x|<\frac\pi 2\sqrt A,\quad y,t\in \mathbb R.  \] This is a complete, properly embedded noncompact surface diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^2$. It has zero Gauss curvature and is invariant under translation in the direction $(0,1,a)$. Its horizontal graph domain is a strip of width $\pi \sqrt{1+a^2}$. The case $a=0$ is the ordinary grim-reaper cylinder. The underlying surface is a rotation and dilation of that cylinder. At a fixed width greater than $\pi $, the two signs of $a$ give the two opposite tilts. Translation in a tangent invariant direction does not change the evolving image. Products with Euclidean factors give higher-dimensional translators. Graphical weighted stability holds, as in the preceding example. See [ CatHIMWGraphical18 ] , equation (1.4), PDF page 3, with exchanged horizontal coordinates and reflected vertical direction. These cylinders must be distinguished from the strictly convex $\Delta $-wings on strips of the same width.

title: 3.3 The rotational bowl translator
text: Example 3.3.1 (The rotational bowl translator) . ECF360A3D482 For each $n\geq 2$, the bowl is the entire graph $z=f(r)$, $r=|x|$ in $\mathbb R^ n$, moving by $z\mapsto z+t$. Its radial profile is specified by the regular ODE \[  \frac{f''}{1+(f')^2}+\frac{n-1}{r}f'=1,\qquad f(0)=f'(0)=0,\qquad f''(0)=1/n.  \] This is an ODE characterization, not an elementary closed formula. The bowl is complete, properly embedded, strictly convex, rotationally invariant, and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. For $n\geq 2$ it has one topological end and gives an eternal flow. Up to a vertical additive constant, its height has asymptotic expansion \[  f(r)=\frac{r^2}{2(n-1)}-\log r+C+O(r^{-1})\quad (r\to \infty ).  \] A paraboloid is only a leading approximation, not the exact translator. It is unique among entire rotationally invariant translating graphs, up to translation. In $\mathbb R^3$ it is the only complete entire translating graph, up to the natural rigid motions and normalization. In $\mathbb R^3$, Brendle–Choi's theorem characterizes its flow among noncompact, strictly convex, noncollapsed ancient flows, up to scaling and ambient isometries. These are the hypotheses of the cited classification. Graphical weighted stability holds. The stronger dynamical stability theorem of Clutterbuck–Schnürer–Schulze concerns continuous graphical initial data whose height difference from the bowl tends to zero at spatial infinity; the resulting height difference tends uniformly to zero as time tends to infinity. The supplied notes [ CatHIMWNotes19 ] , Section 4 and Theorem 4.1, PDF pages 10–11, describe the construction and classification. The original ODE and asymptotic analysis is [ CSS07 ] , Section 2, Lemmas 2.1–2.2; its Theorem 1.1 gives the stated dynamical stability. The ancient classification is [ CatBrendleChoi19 ] , Theorem 1.1, printed page 36 (PDF page 2). The entropy is $\lambda (\mathrm{Bowl}^ n)=\lambda (S^{n-1}(\sqrt{2(n-1)}))$, in particular $\sqrt{2\pi /e}$ in $\mathbb R^3$. This follows from [ CatSunWang2025 ] , Example 3.6 and Corollary 2.4 with Lemma 2.5, PDF pp. 8–11; it is not an identity for the fixed-center Gaussian area of the bowl.

title: 3.4 Rotational translating catenoids
text: Example 3.4.1 (Rotational translating catenoids) . 72E3A9DEA98C For every neck radius $R>0$ and $n\geq 2$, there is a rotational translating hypersurface with two ends. These are also called winglike translators. They move upward with unit speed. A convenient numerical description uses meridian arclength $s$ and tangent angle $\alpha $: \[  r'=\cos \alpha ,\qquad z'=\sin \alpha ,\qquad \alpha '=\cos \alpha -\frac{n-1}{r}\sin \alpha , \qquad (r,z,\alpha )(0)=(R,0,\pi /2).  \] Revolution gives $(r(s)\omega ,z(s)+t)$ with $\omega \in S^{n-1}$ and $t\in \mathbb R$. The arclength system is obtained from $\vec H=e_{n+1}^{\perp }$ and is not a closed formula. The surface is complete, embedded, noncompact and nonconvex, with topology $S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$. In $\mathbb R^3$ it is an annulus, not an entire graph. Outside the neck the two ends are radial graphs. Each has expansion \[  f_\pm (r)=\frac{r^2}{2(n-1)}-\log r+C_\pm +O(r^{-1}).  \] In particular the two ends go to spatial infinity and the complete surface is proper. The parameter controls the neck radius. The supplied survey describes the limiting double bowl with a singular point on the axis as the neck parameter tends to zero. See [ CatHIMWNotes19 ] , Section 4, PDF page 10. The original construction and end expansion are [ CSS07 ] , Lemma 2.3, PDF pages 5–7 of the author preprint. No uniqueness beyond the radial initial-value construction, nor an entropy or stability classification for this non-graphical surface, is asserted here.

title: 3.5 Strictly convex delta-wing translators
text: Example 3.5.1 (Strictly convex delta-wing translators) . B72E7DC6B42E For every $b>\pi /2$, there is a complete strictly convex unit-speed translator that is a graph $z=u_ b(x,y)$ over \[  (x,y)\in \mathbb R\times (-b,b),\qquad \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{(u_ b)_ i(u_ b)_ j}{1+|Du_ b|^2}\right)(u_ b)_{ij}=1.  \] This is a nonlinear PDE characterization; no explicit height formula is supplied. The graph is embedded, noncompact, diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^2$, and has positive Gauss curvature everywhere. After centering and a vertical translation, $u_ b(0,0)=0$ is its minimum and $u_ b$ is even in both coordinates. The width is exactly $2b>\pi $. Among complete translators on this strip that are not tilted grim reapers, it is unique up to translation. The centered solution depends smoothly on compact sets under limits of the width parameter. Along the two unbounded horizontal directions, translated graphs converge smoothly to the two oppositely tilted grim-reaper cylinders of the same strip width. Their angle is determined by \[  \cos \theta =\frac{\pi }{2b}.  \] This relation follows from the explicit tilted-cylinder width; the supplied preprint has an inverted ratio in its printed statement of Theorem 2.4. Graphical weighted stability holds. This is a strictly convex surface, whereas the tilted grim-reaper cylinders on the same strip have zero Gauss curvature. See [ CatHIMWGraphical18 ] , Theorems 1.1, 2.4, 4.1 and 5.7 and Corollary 5.5 (PDF pages 4, 6, 10–12). The construction, uniqueness, and asymptotic results are cited rather than reproduced here. An illustration of the strip and its two limiting grim cylinders is a schematic of its asymptotics, not a computed solution $u_ b$.

title: 3.11 Nonrotational entire convex translators
text: Example 3.11.1 (Nonrotational entire convex translators) . 0F00F9295CD9 In every dimension $n\geq 3$, Xu-Jia Wang constructs entire convex solutions $u:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$ of the unit-speed upward translator equation \[  \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{u_ i u_ j}{1+|Du|^2}\right)u_{ij}=1  \] whose level sets are not spheres or round cylinders in any orthogonal coordinate system. This is an existence construction, not an explicit formula. The graphs are embedded, complete, proper and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$; the last three facts also follow directly from being smooth entire graphs. Their flows exist for all $t\in \mathbb R$ by translation. They are convex and break the spherical or cylindrical rotational pattern of the bowl and its Euclidean products. The corresponding statement for complete entire graphs in $\mathbb R^3$ is false: there the bowl is the only example. Under spatial blow-down $u_ h(x)=h^{-1}u(\sqrt h\, x)$, Wang's theorem gives, after rotations depending on $h$, a quadratic limit of the form \[  \frac{x_1^2+\cdots +x_ k^2}{2(k-1)},\qquad 2\leq k\leq n.  \] The theorem does not rule out slow rotation of the axes as $h\to \infty $. This is an asymptotic limit, not a formula for $u$. The same paper also constructs nonrotational complete convex graphical translators over slab regions. No uniqueness theorem for the general higher-dimensional families is claimed here. See [ CatXJWang11 ] , Theorems 1.2–1.3, printed pages 1187–1188 (PDF pages 3–4), using the case $\sigma =1$ of equation (1.2); the $\sigma =0$ case describes a different, level-set formulation. Any three-dimensional drawing of these higher-dimensional examples is only a projected or sectional schematic.

text: Example 3.6.1 (Translators with prescribed apex curvatures) . D68656E88625 Let $k_1,\ldots ,k_ n\geq 0$ with $\sum _ i k_ i=1$. Hoffman–Ilmanen–Martín–White construct a complete properly embedded translating graph over an open domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$. After reflecting their downward convention to upward translation, it satisfies \[  \min u=u(0)=0,\qquad D^2u(0)=\operatorname {diag}(k_1,\ldots ,k_ n).  \] These equations specify apex data, not an explicit global formula. The function is even in every coordinate. If $k_ i=0$ it is invariant under translation in the $i$-th coordinate; if $k_ i>0$, then $D_ i u$ has the same sign as $x_ i$ away from $x_ i=0$. Equal apex curvatures $k_ i=k_ j$ give invariance under rotations in the $(x_ i,x_ j)$-plane. The domain is either all of $\mathbb R^ n$ or a slab $\{ |x_ i|<b\} $. In the slab case the corresponding $k_ i$ is strictly larger than every other $k_ j$. If the two largest prescribed curvatures are equal, the resulting graph is entire. The supplied edition obtains an $(n-2)$-parameter family of pairwise noncongruent entire examples this way. The construction gives existence and the listed symmetries, but does not assert general uniqueness or convexity of every higher-dimensional graph. In particular, apex positivity alone is not a global convexity theorem. See [ CatHIMWGraphical18 ] , Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 8.2, PDF page 18. The source also has a prescribed-width slab construction in Section 11; its final discussion explicitly leaves general convexity open. A curvature-ellipse illustration displays only the local Hessian data, not the global surface.

title: 3.7 Scherkenoid translators
text: Example 3.7.1 (Scherkenoid translators) . title: 3.8 The pitchfork translator
text: Example 3.8.1 (The pitchfork translator) . B5E7AB44607B The pitchfork is a complete, properly embedded, simply connected, nongraphical translator in $\mathbb R^3$. The supplied notes describe it as a limit of Scherk-type examples, without an explicit formula. It has genus zero. This distinguishes it from Nguyen's periodic infinite-genus tridents despite their similar asymptotic plane arrangements. After reflection to upward translation, it is asymptotic to one plane as $z\to -\infty $ and to three parallel planes as $z\to +\infty $. These are height-direction asymptotics, not a claim that the surface has four topological ends. Its translation yields an eternal noncompact flow. The later construction paper records finite topology and quadratic area growth for its pitchfork subfamily. See [ CatHIMWNotes19 ] , Section 5 and Figure 7, PDF pages 11–12, and [ CatHMW20 ] . The existence proof is external. The supplied notes do not give a complete parameter range or a uniqueness theorem, and the plane diagram is only schematic.

title: 3.10 Finite-genus translators with three ends
text: Example 3.10.1 (Finite-genus translators with three ends) . 85D3C19BE7E6 Dávila–del Pino–Nguyen construct complete embedded orientable translating surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ with finite topology and large genus. title: 3.12 Translators with an Angenent-torus end
text: Example 3.12.1 (Translators with an Angenent-torus end) . BF18BDD64F8E Let $S_ A\subset \mathbb R^3$ be an embedded Angenent self-shrinking torus, normalized by $\vec H_{S_ A}=-X^\perp /2$. Sun–Wang construct complete embedded three-dimensional translators $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^4=\mathbb R^3_ x\times \mathbb R_ z$ satisfying \[  \vec H_\Sigma =e_4^\perp ,\qquad M_ t=\Sigma +t e_4,\qquad -\infty <t<\infty .  \] These are variationally constructed hypersurfaces, not explicit parametrized solutions. At sufficiently large height each has the exact graph representation \[  \Sigma \cap \{ z\geq z_0\}  =\left\{ \left(\sqrt z\, [x+u(x,z)\nu _ A(x)],z\right): x\in S_ A,\  z\geq z_0\right\} ,\qquad \| u(\cdot ,z)\| _{C^0(S_ A)}=O(z^{-\epsilon })  \] for some $\epsilon >0$. The unknown function $u$ is solved for by the construction. In particular, the auxiliary expression obtained by setting $u=0$ is not asserted to be a translator. The translators have codimension one and are smooth, noncompact, complete, and properly embedded. Sun–Wang's general construction can have a singular set of dimension at most $n-7$ for an $n$-dimensional translator in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$; for the present $n=3$ this set is empty. There is a compact core and one end diffeomorphic to $S_ A\times [z_0,\infty )$. Thus a fixed time slice has one topological end, and its sufficiently high horizontal cross-sections have genus one. The translator is a three-manifold: a surface genus is not assigned to it, and the theorem does not identify its compact core as a solid torus. Its unique tangent flow at backward infinity is the multiplicity-one shrinking cylinder generated by $S_ A\times \mathbb R$. Equivalently, \[  R^{-1/2}(\Sigma -R e_4)\longrightarrow S_ A\times \mathbb R \quad \hbox{as }R\longrightarrow \infty .  \] This parabolic blow-down cylinder and the single topological end are different notions. Write $I_ A=\operatorname {ind}_{F}(S_ A)$ for the number of negative eigenvalues of \[  -L_{S_ A},\qquad L_{S_ A}=\Delta _{S_ A}-\tfrac 12 X^\top \! \cdot \nabla _{S_ A} +|A_{S_ A}|^2+\tfrac 12,  \] counted with multiplicity. The translating ends have an $I_ A$-parameter construction, indexed by a ball in $\mathbb R^{I_ A}$ for each sufficiently large cutoff. No exact numerical value of $I_ A$ is needed here. These parameters include ambient translations; they are not a count of parameters after quotienting by rigid motions. The completions need not form a smooth or single-valued family across a fattening parameter. A rotationally invariant subfamily can be chosen. The chosen completions minimize Ilmanen's weighted area $\mathcal I=\int e^ z\, d\mathcal H^3$ locally with their boundary fixed. Consequently they are stable for compactly supported variations of that weighted functional. This statement is not a claim of entropy stability or dynamical stability under mean curvature flow. Their entropy is finite and satisfies the exact identity \[  \lambda (\Sigma )=F(S_ A\times \mathbb R)=F(S_ A)=\lambda (S_ A) =\frac1{4\pi }\int _{S_ A}e^{-|x|^2/4}\, d\mathcal H^2.  \] No closed numerical value or value of $F_{0,1}(\Sigma )$ is supplied by this construction. Nonuniqueness occurs within this same family. There is a rotationally invariant translating end $\Sigma _ e$ for which the associated closed set $T[\Sigma _ e]$ has nonempty interior and \[  \partial T[\Sigma _ e]=T^+\sqcup T^-.  \] The two distinct boundary hypersurfaces are complete smooth embedded $\mathcal I$-minimizing translators, exponentially asymptotic to the same $\Sigma _ e$. Their normalized graph difference decays exponentially in height. This is nonuniqueness of minimizing completions of a fixed end; it is not an assertion that there are exactly two arbitrary translators with that end. For the fixed ball of ends supplied by the construction, the parameters at which fattening occurs form a meager subset. Off that subset there is a unique $\mathcal I$-minimizing completion exponentially asymptotic to the specified end. The uniqueness statement is restricted to this minimizing class and this asymptotic condition. The original torus is constructed in [ CatAngenent1992 ] , unnumbered theorem on PDF page 1 of the supplied preprint; its original normalization is converted by multiplying the reference immersion by $\sqrt2$. The translator construction is [ CatSunWang2025 ] , Theorems 1.1 and 3.7 (PDF pages 2 and 12), Theorem 4.1 (page 28), and Theorem 4.3 (pages 32–34). The compact-core and single-end statement follows from Lemma 2.5 and the graphical end description in Lemma 3.2 (pages 9–10). The entropy identity is Corollary 2.4 and Lemma 2.5 (pages 8–9). Fattening and its genericity are Theorem 5.1 (page 35, proved on pages 38–39) and Corollary 4.5 (page 34). The construction is not an exhaustive classification, and its realization as a type-II blow-up of a closed flow is stated as Conjecture 4.6 in that paper.
