title: 3.13 Translators with high-genus spherical-doubling ends
text: Example 3.13.1 (Translators with high-genus spherical-doubling ends) . 9B1B88A4317F Fix an integer $m$ sufficiently large. In the spherical-doubling construction of Kapouleas–McGrath, choose two latitude circles and $m$ aligned bridge sites on each circle. Their theorem gives a smooth closed embedded shrinker $S_ m\subset \mathbb R^3$, obtained by connecting two nearby copies of the radius-two sphere with $2m$ small catenoidal bridges. Its genus is $2m-1$. This specifies a concrete subfamily of their construction; there is no effective lower threshold for $m$ or explicit formula for $S_ m$ in this statement. Applying the Sun–Wang construction to $S_ m$ produces complete embedded translators $\Sigma _ m^3\subset \mathbb R^4$ with \[  \vec H_{\Sigma _ m}=e_4^\perp ,\qquad M_ t=\Sigma _ m+t e_4,\quad t\in \mathbb R,  \] and, outside a compact set, \[  \Sigma _ m= \left\{ \left(\sqrt z\, [x+u_ m(x,z)\nu _{S_ m}(x)],z\right): x\in S_ m,\  z\geq z_0\right\} ,\qquad \| u_ m(\cdot ,z)\| _{C^0(S_ m)}=O(z^{-\epsilon _ m})  \] for some $\epsilon _ m>0$. Both the shrinker and the translator are existence constructions; the displayed formula contains an unknown correction and is not an explicit solution. Each translator is a smooth, complete, properly embedded, noncompact hypersurface, with one end diffeomorphic to $S_ m\times [z_0,\infty )$. The genus $2m-1$ belongs to the two-dimensional horizontal cross-section. No surface genus or complete three-manifold topology is assigned to $\Sigma _ m$. The unique tangent flow at backward infinity is generated by $S_ m\times \mathbb R$ with multiplicity one. Thus these examples have a different prescribed shrinker from the Angenent-torus-end examples, the bowl, and the previously catalogued three-ended translating surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$. For each fixed $S_ m$ the end construction has $I_ m=\operatorname {ind}_ F(S_ m)$ parameters before quotienting by ambient translations. The exact index is not computed by the cited construction. One may choose an end and a minimizing completion invariant under the finite symmetry group $\mathcal G_ m=D_{2m}\times \mathbb Z_2$ of order $4m$, where $D_{2m}$ here denotes the dihedral group of order $2m$. Symmetry is asserted for such selected examples, not for every member of the full $I_ m$-parameter family. The completions are locally $\mathcal I$-minimizing for $\mathcal I=\int e^ z\, d\mathcal H^3$, hence stable for compactly supported variations of that functional. The generic uniqueness result concerns minimizing completions exponentially asymptotic to a fixed constructed end. No specific fattening example for these $S_ m$ is proved in the cited sources. The entropy is exactly the Gaussian area of the prescribed shrinker: \[  \lambda (\Sigma _ m)=F(S_ m)=\lambda (S_ m)<2F(S^2(2))=\frac8e.  \] The strict upper bound follows by applying the area inequality of Kapouleas–McGrath in the Gaussian metric $g=e^{-|x|^2/4}g_{\rm Euc}$ and dividing its surface area by $4\pi $. It is a consequence of the two cited theorems, not a numerical approximation. No individual numerical entropy or value of $F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ m)$ is recorded. For the input shrinkers, see [ CatKapouleasMcGrath2023 ] , Theorem 10.5, with $k_\circ =2$ and $\mathbf m=(m)$ (arXiv version 4, PDF page 66), Theorem 9.40 (page 65), and Definitions 7.10–7.11 and Remark 7.12 (page 40). The genus is $|L|-1=2m-1$; smooth embeddedness and the Gaussian-metric area inequality follow from Theorem 5.7 and equation (5.9) (page 30; also Theorem A on page 3). The application to translators uses [ CatSunWang2025 ] , Theorems 3.7 and 4.1 (pages 12 and 28), with compact core and entropy as in Lemma 2.5 and Corollary 2.4 (pages 8–10). This spherical-doubling specialization uses the explicit nondegeneracy check for the radius-two sphere in Section 10; it does not require the separate Angenent-torus doubling theorem of Kapouleas–McGrath.

title: 4.1 Expanding smoothings of planar corners
text: The convention throughout these entries is $\vec H=X^\perp /2$ for the time-one profile. Thus $M_ t=\sqrt t\, M$, $t>0$, is the corresponding flow. The positive weight for variational statements is $e^{|X|^2/4}$; minimizing this weighted area locally will be called $E$-minimizing. Example 4.1.1 (Even graphical corner expanders) . 72808FA576A9 For every $\kappa >0$ there is a smooth even function $\phi _\kappa :\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ satisfying \[  \frac{\phi _\kappa ''}{1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2} +\frac{x\phi _\kappa '-\phi _\kappa }{2}=0, \qquad \phi _\kappa '(0)=0, \qquad \lim _{|x|\to \infty }\frac{\phi _\kappa (x)}{|x|}=\kappa .  \] The profile $\Gamma _\kappa =\{ (x,\phi _\kappa (x)):x\in \mathbb R\} $ is a smooth complete properly embedded noncompact curve in $\mathbb R^2$, with topology $\mathbb R$, reflection symmetry, and two ends asymptotic to the rays of $y=\kappa |x|$. It is $E$-minimizing against compact replacements. Its curvature vector is nonzero and points along the upward graph normal: writing $q=\phi _\kappa -x\phi _\kappa '$ gives $q'=-x(1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2)q/2$ and $\phi _\kappa ''=(1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2)q/2$, with $q(0)>0$. The source gives the quantitative estimate, for $x>0$, \[  0\leq \phi _\kappa (x)-\kappa x \leq \min \left\{ \frac{2e(\kappa +2)}{x}e^{-x^2/4},\, 3\kappa +2\right\} .  \] The flow $\sqrt t\, \Gamma _\kappa $, $t\in (0,\infty )$, smooths the corner at time zero. These are ODE-defined profiles, not elementary closed formulas. Source: [ CatDing20 ] , Section 4, equations (4.9)–(4.15), printed pp. 373–374, supplied PDF pp. 15–16. The figure shows a numerical ODE profile with $\phi (0)=1$. Taking the product with $\mathbb R$ gives an example in $\mathbb R^3$ with one zero principal curvature.

text: Example 4.3.1 (Entire radial cone smoothings) . D3CC5E948716 For $n\geq 2$ and $\kappa >0$, consider \[  M_\kappa =\{ (x,\phi _\kappa (|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\} \subset \mathbb R^{n+1},  \] where $\phi _\kappa $ is the smooth radial solution constructed with \[  \frac{\phi _\kappa ''}{1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2} +\frac{n-1}{r}\phi _\kappa ' +\frac{r\phi _\kappa '-\phi _\kappa }{2}=0, \qquad \phi _\kappa '(0)=0, \qquad \lim _{r\to \infty }\frac{\phi _\kappa (r)}r=\kappa .  \] The equation at $r=0$ is interpreted by smooth radial extension; it implies $\phi _\kappa ''(0)=\phi _\kappa (0)/(2n)$. This is an ODE construction, not a closed formula. The hypersurface is smooth, complete, properly embedded, noncompact, rotationally symmetric, diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$, and $E$-minimizing against compact replacements. It has one conical end and nondecreasing height. The estimate \[  0\leq \phi _\kappa (r)-\kappa r \leq ((n+1)\kappa +2)\min \{ 1,r^{-1}\} ,\qquad r>0,  \] records the rate at which it approaches its cone. Its flow is $M_ t=\sqrt t\, M_\kappa $ for $t>0$, with initial cone $z=\kappa |x|$. Source: [ CatDing20 ] , Section 4, equations (4.1), (4.7), and (4.8), printed pp. 371–373, supplied PDF pp. 13–15. title: 4.4 Two-sheeted expanders of rotational double cones
search_title: Two-sheeted expanders of rotational double cones
section: 4.4 Two-sheeted expanders of rotational double cones
text: Example 4.4.1 (Disconnected double-cone smoothings) . 4F35D93CA4BD Let $n\geq 2$, write $(x,z)\in \mathbb R^ n\times \mathbb R$, and let \[  D_\alpha =\{ (x,z):|x|=|z|\tan \alpha \} ,\qquad 0<\alpha <\pi /2.  \] With $\phi _{\cot \alpha }$ from Example 4.3.1 , the two-sheeted expander is \[  M_\alpha ^{(2)} =\{ (x,\phi _{\cot \alpha }(|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\}  \mathbin {\cup } \{ (x,-\phi _{\cot \alpha }(|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\} .  \] This display specifies the surface using ODE-defined functions. Its two components are smooth, complete, properly embedded convex entire graphs, each diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. The union is noncompact, invariant under rotations about the $z$-axis and under $z\mapsto -z$, and has two oppositely directed conical ends. The flow $\sqrt t\, M_\alpha ^{(2)}$, $t>0$, approaches $D_\alpha $ as $t\downarrow 0$. Existence and uniqueness of each rotational single-lobe graphical profile are established in [ CatAIC95 ] , Lemma 2(i), printed p. 1947, supplied PDF p. 12. Theorem 4, printed pp. 1950–1951, PDF pp. 15–16, provides a critical angle $\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)\in (0,\pi /2)$. For $\alpha <\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)$ the level-set flow of the double cone is exactly the two-sheeted flow. For angles above this threshold there are also connected smoothings, so the graphical uniqueness statement does not assert uniqueness among all flows from the cone. The critical-angle decimal estimates later in that paper are numerical. The $n=2$ figure rotates two reflected numerical profiles; the cone is their asymptotic limit.

text: Example 4.5.1 (Connected double-cone smoothings) . 3A4775A9BD2C For $n\geq 2$ and a neck parameter $a>0$, the initial value problem \[  u''=(1+(u')^2)\left(\frac{n-1}{u}+\frac{u-zu'}2\right), \qquad u(0)=a,\quad u'(0)=0,  \] defines a positive, smooth, even profile on $\mathbb R$. Rotating it gives \[  M_ a=\{ (u(z)\omega ,z):z\in \mathbb R,\  \omega \in S^{n-1}\}  \subset \mathbb R^{n+1}.  \] This is a smooth complete properly embedded noncompact expander with topology $S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$, rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, and two conical ends. The profile is increasing for $z>0$. Its limiting aperture depends on $a$; the formula is an ODE specification, not an elementary expression. The evolution is $\sqrt t\, M_ a$ for $t>0$. For every $\alpha >\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)$ there exists such a connected expander asymptotic to $D_\alpha $ from Example 4.4.1 . It gives a second thin evolution from that cone alongside the disconnected two-sheeted solution. The cited theorem uses a strict inequality and does not establish a universal uniqueness assertion for the one-sheeted profile. Source: [ CatAIC95 ] , Lemma 2(ii), Lemma 3, and Theorem 4, printed pp. 1947–1951, supplied PDF pp. 12–16. These qualitative expander statements are proved in the source; its separate computed higher-genus shrinker and numerical threshold estimates are not needed here. text: Example 4.6.1 (Ding's smooth minimizing expanders) . A6044506F79A Let $C\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be an $n$-dimensional $C^{3,\beta }$-regular cone, $0<\beta <1$, regular away from its vertex, with a $C^{3,\beta }$ embedded link in $S^ n$. Assume that $C$ is mean convex but not area minimizing, that $\partial \Omega =C$, and that its mean curvature vector points into the chosen domain $\Omega $ wherever it is nonzero. Then there is a unique smooth complete embedded $E$-minimizing self-expanding hypersurface $M\subset \Omega $ with tangent cone $C$ at infinity. Its mean curvature vector is everywhere nonzero and points into $\Omega $, and \[  \{ \sqrt t\, M:t>0\}   \] is a foliation of $\Omega $ moving by mean curvature flow. The normalization is $\vec H=X^\perp /2$. This is an existence theorem for a family determined by the cone and the chosen side, not an explicit parametrization. The uniqueness just stated includes the chosen-side and minimizing hypotheses. Its topology, symmetry, and number of ends depend on the chosen cone. Source: [ CatDing20 ] , Theorem 1.1, printed p. 361, supplied PDF p. 3, and Theorem 6.12, printed pp. 402–403, PDF pp. 44–45. The broader minimizing-current existence theorem in that paper can have singularities and is not being substituted for this smooth theorem. title: 4.2 Self-expanding planar tree networks
text: Example 4.2.1 (Regular expanding trees with prescribed rays) . 16898F334139 A regular planar network consists of smooth branches meeting only at triple junctions, with angles $120$ degrees at every junction. A self-expanding network $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^2$ satisfies \[  \vec k=\frac{X^\perp }{2}  \] on each open branch; its time evolution is $\Sigma _ t=\sqrt t\, \Sigma $, $t>0$, with the same angle condition. It is a network flow and is not a smooth immersed curve at its junctions. For finitely many distinct prescribed rays from the origin, connected tree-like expanders provide smoothings in this network sense. Existence for three rays, including uniqueness of the tree, and existence for more rays are recalled in [ CatINS19 ] , Section 7, printed p. 70, supplied PDF p. 32, with attribution there to Schnürer–Schulze and Mazzeo–Sáez respectively. The branches can be described as geodesics for the conformal metric \[  g=e^{|X|^2/2}(dX_1^2+dX_2^2),  \] with the junction balance condition. Noncompact ends approach their assigned rays with Gaussian decay. Two regular expanders with the same asymptotic rays coincide if they are in the same topological class: the comparison deformation must retain distinct junctions and the prescribed asymptotic ends, as in the source definition. This does not assert uniqueness across different network topologies. See [ CatINS19 ] , Lemmas 4.1 and 4.3 and Theorem 4.4, printed pp. 49–51, supplied PDF pp. 11–13. The source uses $\vec k=\psi ^\perp $ and $\sqrt{2t}\, \psi $; our profile is $\Sigma =\sqrt2\, \psi $. Nontrivial networks arise from a geodesic boundary-value construction. The exact balanced special case \[  \bigcup _{j=0}^2\{ r(\cos (2\pi j/3),\sin (2\pi j/3)):r\geq 0\}   \] is the stationary $Y$ network. It illustrates the junction condition. The accompanying general tree diagram is schematic; its branches are not numerically solved.

section: 5.2 The catenoid as an eternal stationary flow
text: Example 5.2.1 (Stationary catenoid flow) . AC1C0D984A58 For $a>0$ the explicit immersion \[  X(\theta ,s,t)=a(\cosh s\cos \theta ,\cosh s\sin \theta ,s), \quad \theta \in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z,\quad s\in \mathbb R,\quad t\in \mathbb R,  \] is independent of time and has $\vec H=0$. It is therefore an eternal stationary mean curvature flow in $\mathbb R^3$. Every time slice is a complete properly embedded noncompact rotational annulus, with two ends and a waist circle of radius $a$. Its metric and curvature are \[  g=a^2\cosh ^2s(d\theta ^2+ds^2),\qquad K=-\frac1{a^2\cosh ^4s},\qquad \int K\, dA=-4\pi .  \] The metric follows by differentiation, and the conformal curvature formula gives $K$ and its integral. The complete catenoid is unstable for compactly supported area variations: for a test function $f(s)$ independent of $\theta $, its second variation is \[  Q(f,f)=2\pi \int _{\mathbb R}\bigl ((f')^2-2\operatorname {sech}^2s\, f^2\bigr )\, ds.  \] Taking $f$ equal to one on $[-R,R]$, zero outside $[-2R,2R]$, and $|f'|\leq C/R$ makes this negative for large $R$. Each open half is a minimal graph over $r>a$, with $z=\pm a\operatorname {arcosh}(r/a)$, so it is stable for compactly supported variations in that half. These are minimal-area stability assertions, not a classification of dynamical stability under MCF. The supplied source also records the catenoid in [ CatMan11 ] , Remark 4.4.7, printed p. 105, supplied PDF p. 116. The parametrization is exact and supports interactive rotation, scale selection, and a truncated height range with the omitted infinite ends stated.

section: 5.6 Mean curvature evolution of the Whitney sphere
text: Example 5.6.1 (A collapsing Lagrangian immersed sphere) . 245DFF2BED27 For $n\geq 2$, the initial Whitney immersion in $\mathbb R^{2n}=\mathbb C^ n$ is explicitly \[  F_0(x_1,\ldots ,x_{n+1}) =\frac{(x_1,x_1x_{n+1},\ldots ,x_ n,x_ nx_{n+1})}{1+x_{n+1}^2}, \qquad (x_1,\ldots ,x_{n+1})\in S^ n.  \] It is a compact Lagrangian immersion, of dimension and codimension $n$, with one transverse double image point at the origin coming from the two poles. It is complete and proper as an immersion of a compact domain, and it is not embedded. Its equivariance reduces the geometry to the planar initial profile \[  \gamma _0(u)=\left(\frac{\sin u}{1+\cos ^2u}, \frac{\sin u\cos u}{1+\cos ^2u}\right), \qquad u\in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z.  \] For $n\geq 2$ the profile evolution is the equivariant equation \[  (\partial _ t\gamma )^\perp =\vec k-(n-1)\frac{\gamma ^\perp }{|\gamma |^2},  \] interpreted by the smooth equivariant immersion at the double point. It is not ordinary planar curve shortening. The maximal smooth mean curvature flow $F_ t$, $t\in [0,T)$, remains Lagrangian and equivariant. It collapses to the origin in finite time, and its tangent flow there is a Lagrangian plane with multiplicity two. The Whitney sphere is not a self-similar solution. These statements are the special case stated in [ CatViana18 ] , pp. 1–3, especially the result on p. 2 and Theorem 1.3 on p. 3. The formulas above specify the initial geometry and its reduced equation, not a closed expression for $F_ t$ at positive time. The figure shows the exact initial generating profile $\gamma _0$ of this higher-codimension immersion.

text: Example 5.3.1 (Angenent–Velázquez type-II singularities) . 922034E946EB Let $n\geq 2$, let $m\geq 3$ be odd, and let $K>0$. section: 5.1 The Angenent oval as an explicit ancient flow
text: Example 5.1.1 (The ancient paperclip curve) . B008243C5D96 With the speed-one curve-shortening convention, the exact implicit equation \[  \Gamma _ t=\{ (x,y)\in \mathbb R^2:|x|<\pi /2,\  e^ t\cosh y=\cos x\} , \qquad -\infty <t<0,  \] defines the Angenent oval. Equivalently, its two graph branches are \[  y=\pm \operatorname {arcosh}(e^{-t}\cos x), \qquad |x|\leq \arccos (e^ t).  \] Their endpoints join smoothly as a curve, even though those graph charts cease to be regular there. This is an exact implicit formula, rather than a single global graph parametrization. It is recorded in [ BV11 ] , Section 3.1, equation (14), p. 7. Every time slice is a smooth compact embedded strictly convex curve, hence complete and proper, with topology $S^1$ and reflection symmetries across both coordinate axes. It shrinks to the origin at time zero but changes shape and is not a soliton. Its enclosed area is $-2\pi t$, and \[  \kappa _{\max }=(1-e^{2t})^{-1/2},\qquad \kappa _{\min }=e^ t(1-e^{2t})^{-1/2}.  \] The rescaling $(-t)^{-1/2}\Gamma _ t$ converges smoothly to the radius-$\sqrt2$ circle at extinction. As $t\to -\infty $, translating its upper and lower branches to keep their tips fixed gives the two oppositely directed grim-reaper profiles, locally in $|x|<\pi /2$. These limits can be read from the implicit equation: near extinction its quadratic expansion gives $x^2+y^2\sim -2t$, and subtracting the upper tip height gives the limiting graph $\log \cos x$ as $t\to -\infty $. The time slider plots the exact implicit curve for $-5\leq t\leq -0.1$ on a fixed spatial scale.

text: Example 5.7.1 (Compact ancient torus curves) . D28FAF32B556 Fix $m\geq 2$ and integers $1=k_1<k_2<\cdots <k_ m$. For $t<0$, let $r(t)>0$ be the unique solution of \[  \sum _{j=1}^ m r(t)^{2k_ j^2}=-2t.  \] Then the exact parametrization \[  \gamma _ t(\theta )= \bigl (r(t)^{k_1^2}\cos (k_1\theta ),r(t)^{k_1^2}\sin (k_1\theta ), \ldots ,r(t)^{k_ m^2}\cos (k_ m\theta ),r(t)^{k_ m^2}\sin (k_ m\theta )\bigr ), \qquad \theta \in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z,  \] is an ancient curve-shortening flow in $\mathbb R^{2m}$. Its scale is specified by an exact implicit equation; no elementary inverse in time is required. Equivalently, \[  r'=-\frac{r}{\sum _ j k_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2}}.  \] Each time slice is a compact smooth embedded circle, hence complete and proper, with no ends and codimension $2m-1$. Embeddedness follows directly from $k_1=1$, because the first two coordinates already determine $\theta $. The name refers to a curve lying on a product of circles, not to a two-dimensional torus. It spans $\mathbb R^{2m}$, has a one-parameter simultaneous rotational symmetry, and is non-self-similar when $m\geq 2$ because the ratios of its different coordinate radii change with time. The rescaled curves $(-t)^{-1/2}\gamma _ t$ tend to the radius-$\sqrt2$ circle with multiplicity $k_ m$ as $t\to -\infty $, and with multiplicity one as $t\uparrow 0$. Stryker–Sun prove \[  \sup _{t<0}\lambda (\gamma _ t)=k_ m\lambda (S^1) =k_ m\sqrt{\frac{2\pi }{e}},  \] which also bounds the entropy of every time slice. This is a supremum over time, not a formula for the entropy at each finite time. For the fixed center and Gaussian scale, direct integration gives \[  F_{0,1}(\gamma _ t)=\sqrt\pi \left(\sum _ j k_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2}\right)^{1/2}e^{t/2}.  \] Indeed, $|\gamma _ t|^2=-2t$ and $|\partial _\theta \gamma _ t|^2=\sum _ jk_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2}$. The centered Gaussian area is distinct from the supremum defining $\lambda $. Source: [ CatSS19 ] , equation (2.1), Propositions 2.1–2.2, Corollary 2.3, and Theorem A.1, PDF pp. 3–5 and 8–9. The general source formula allows $k_1>1$; if the frequencies have common divisor $d>1$, that parametrization is a $d$-fold cover and its mass counts multiplicity. The embedded subfamily above avoids this ambiguity. The construction was already present in [ CatAAAW13 ] , Section 3, equations (11)–(14), PDF pp. 8–9, as acknowledged in [ CatSS19 ] , Remark 1.3. The interactive figure uses $(k_1,k_2)=(1,2)$ in $\mathbb R^4$. Its three-coordinate display is a projection, with time and fourth-coordinate rotation controls.

title: 5.4 Eternal shrinking helices
text: Example 5.4.1 (Helical curve-shortening flows) . 1EF23C4EFFC0 Fix $m\geq 1$ and integers $1\leq k_1<\cdots <k_ m$. Let $r(t)>0$, $t\in \mathbb R$, solve the exact implicit equation \[  \log r(t)+\frac12\sum _{j=1}^ m r(t)^{2k_ j^2}=\frac m2-t.  \] The choice of constant makes $r(0)=1$. Then \[  \Gamma _ t(s)= \bigl (r^{k_1^2}\cos (k_1s),r^{k_1^2}\sin (k_1s),\ldots , r^{k_ m^2}\cos (k_ ms),r^{k_ m^2}\sin (k_ ms),s\bigr ), \qquad s\in \mathbb R,  \] is an eternal curve-shortening flow in $\mathbb R^{2m+1}$. In the simplest case $m=1$, $k_1=1$, it is the three-dimensional helix \[  \Gamma _ t(s)=(r(t)\cos s,r(t)\sin s,s),\qquad \log r(t)+r(t)^2/2=1/2-t.  \] These are exact parametrizations with an implicitly determined time scale, not numerical ODE profiles. The ordinary differential equation is \[  r'=-\frac{r}{1+\sum _ j k_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2}}.  \] The last coordinate makes every time slice a proper embedding of $\mathbb R$, and the induced metric is $(1+\sum _ jk_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2})ds^2$, so it is complete. It is noncompact with two ends and codimension $2m$, and it spans the stated ambient space. Simultaneous rotations together with translation along the last coordinate give its screw symmetry. Its radius decreases to zero as $t\to +\infty $, giving local smooth convergence to the axis, while $r(t)\to \infty $ as $t\to -\infty $. At any fixed finite time the ends continue winding; they are not asymptotic to the axis as $|s|\to \infty $. Proposition 2.7 of [ CatSS19 ] proves \[  \sup _{t\in \mathbb R}\lambda (\Gamma _ t)=+\infty .  \] This concerns the entire time family and does not say that every individual slice has infinite entropy. In fact, a direct calculation gives the exact fixed-time entropy below. Set $B=\sum _ jr^{2k_ j^2}$ and $D=\sum _ jk_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2}$. Direct Gaussian integration, using $|\Gamma _ t(s)|^2=B+s^2$, gives the exact centered value \[  F_{0,1}(\Gamma _ t)=\sqrt{1+D}\, e^{-B/4}; \qquad F_{0,1}(\Gamma _ t)=\sqrt{1+r^2}\, e^{-r^2/4} \quad \hbox{when }m=k_1=1.  \] For completeness, the same calculation at arbitrary Gaussian scale gives \[  \lambda (\Gamma _ t)=\sqrt{1+D(t)}.  \] Indeed, for a center $(a,z_0)\in \mathbb R^{2m}\times \mathbb R$, dropping the nonnegative squared distance in the first $2m$ coordinates bounds $F_{(a,z_0),\tau }$ by $(4\pi \tau )^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+D}\int _{\mathbb R}e^{-(s-z_0)^2/(4\tau )}\, ds=\sqrt{1+D}$. At the origin, $F_{0,\tau }=\sqrt{1+D}e^{-B/(4\tau )}$ tends to this upper bound as $\tau \to \infty $. Thus every finite-time helix has finite entropy, while the time supremum is infinite. This is a direct integration, additional to the cited time-supremum result. Source: [ CatSS19 ] , equation (2.6), Propositions 2.6–2.7, and Theorem A.2, PDF pp. 6–7 and 9; see also [ CatAAAW13 ] , Section 3, PDF pp. 8–10. The interactive three-dimensional figure uses the simplest exact helix, with a time slider and the displayed range $-5\pi /2\leq s\leq 5\pi /2$. The family is eternal even though a display uses only finitely many turns.

text: Example 5.5.1 (Chen–Sun's noncompact multiplicity-two limit) . A50018836027 Chen and Sun construct a nonstatic immortal mean curvature flow $M_ t\subset \mathbb R^3$, $t\in [0,\infty )$, smooth for $t>0$, of connected embedded rotational surfaces. It is also symmetric across the limiting plane. Each positive-time slice consists of two increasing radial graphs joined smoothly at a neck of radius $a(t)>0$: \[  M_ t=\{ (\rho \cos \theta ,\rho \sin \theta ,\pm f(\rho ,t)): \rho \geq a(t),\  \theta \in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z\} .  \] This is a description of the constructed PDE solution, not an explicit formula for $f$. Away from the neck its upper graph satisfies \[  f_ t=\frac{f_{\rho \rho }}{1+f_\rho ^2}+\frac{f_\rho }{\rho }.  \] Near the neck, the inverse graph $\rho =u(z,t)$ instead satisfies \[  u_ t=\frac{u_{zz}}{1+u_ z^2}-\frac1u,\qquad u_ z(0,t)=0.  \] The proof selects a critical initial surface by interpolation among rotational surfaces in finite cylinders and then takes a limit as the cylinder radius tends to infinity. Its initial trace is locally Lipschitz; choosing any positive time as the initial time gives an entirely smooth immortal flow. No closed formula, canonical parameter value, or uniqueness of the constructed critical flow is supplied. The two graphical ends and the smooth connecting neck give topology $S^1\times \mathbb R$: genus zero and two ends. Properness follows from the graphs escaping to infinite radius; the smooth connected surface is complete. It remains in a fixed slab, and the two ends stay asymptotic to their original parallel planes. The neck radius tends to zero only as $t\to \infty $. On compact regions the flow converges to the middle plane with multiplicity two; the two sheets converge smoothly away from the origin. The convergence is not uniform over the entire noncompact surface. This is an infinite-time limit of the unrescaled flow, not a multiplicity-two finite-time tangent flow of a closed embedded surface. text: Example 5.8.1 (Chen–Sun's product-manifold construction) . 225751B3C7E8 For each $n\geq 2$, there is a smooth connected embedded immortal mean curvature flow of compact hypersurfaces in the product manifold \[  (S^ n\times [-1,1],\  g_{S^ n}+dy^2),  \] where $S^ n$ has unit round radius. The flow is defined for all $t\geq 0$ and is nonstatic. Its hypersurface dimension is $n$ and its codimension in this ambient manifold is one. The construction stays in the smaller band $|y|\leq 1/(2n)$, so the same flow is contained in $S^ n\times \mathbb R$; it can also be placed in the closed product $S^ n\times (\mathbb R/4\mathbb Z)$ without changing the metric near the flow. Away from the north and south poles, the two sheets converge smoothly; the two necks collapse only at infinite time.
